harder.verification_criterion: The answer defines what leaching carbon loss is, including the mechanism by which dissolved organic or inorganic carbon is transported from soil through water movement.

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of what “leaching carbon loss” means across ecosystems, with mechanisms, magnitudes, controls, and mitigation options grounded in current evidence.

Definitions and pathways
- Leaching carbon loss refers to the transfer of organic carbon (primarily dissolved organic carbon, DOC) and, in some systems, inorganic carbon (e.g., carbonates) from soils or sediments into water via soil solution, where it can be transported off-site and ultimately respired to CO2 or emitted as methane (CH4) in anaerobic conditions. <cite id="29bff118-2">Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-4">DOC is a mobile soil carbon pool that can be adsorbed, retained, or transported by soil water into the water column</cite>.
- Mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC/MAOM) forms relatively stable associations with clays and iron oxides, but dissolution of minerals or changes in mineral chemistry can mobilize this carbon into more labile, leachable forms. <cite id="faaccd23-0">Mineral-associated organic carbon can constitute up to about 81% of bulk soil organic carbon, with protection by clays and Fe oxides enhancing stability</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-1">Dissolution of minerals by organic ligands (e.g., oxalic acid), root exudates, and reductive dissolution of Fe/Mn can transform mineral-associated organic carbon to accessible forms, priming microbial decomposition and release into solution</cite>.

Magnitude of leaching losses and system controls
- Quantitatively, leaching can rival a nontrivial fraction of net ecosystem carbon exchange in many ecosystems. <cite id="29bff118-2">Soil carbon leached from forests, grasslands, and croplands across Europe was estimated at 15.1, 32.4, and 20.5 g C m−2 yr−1, corresponding to 4%, 14%, and 8% of net ecosystem exchange, respectively</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-2">In arid and semiarid regions, soil inorganic carbon is particularly prone to leaching during sporadic high precipitation events</cite>.
- Hydrology and storm events are key triggers. <cite id="29bff118-2">Very little detailed data exists to compare respiration and leaching, yet extreme precipitation can enhance both, with leaching especially important under episodic wetting in drier regions</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-3">In a lateritic Ultisol under tropical rainfall simulated in columns, leaching accounted for 1.4% of added carbon while respiration accounted for 10.4%, with sandy texture increasing leachate losses; a subtropical regime favored respiration</cite>.
- Depth, adsorption, and time dependence shape losses. <cite id="29bff118-4">DOC in leachate generally increases with soil depth and declines with leaching time due to adsorption and retention in lower layers; upper layers lose more TOC initially, and retention capacity varies with mineralogy and organic matter quality</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-1">First-order kinetics describe DOC leaching with a characteristic half-life, enabling estimation of remaining leachable C as a function of time</cite>.

Mechanisms: MAOC stability and mobilization
- Protection vs. vulnerability. <cite id="faaccd23-0">Associations with Fe/Al oxides and certain clays confer high stability to mineral-associated organic carbon, with over 36% of mineral-associated carbon persisting under strong chemical oxidation, evidencing protection efficacy</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-1">However, mineral dissolution driven by organic ligands, microbes, and redox reactions can liberate carbon, converting protected pools into more accessible and leachable forms</cite>.
- Chemical and biological levers. <cite id="faaccd23-1">Oxalic acid and other organic ligands can chelate minerals, root exudates can destabilize associations, and reductive dissolution of Fe/Mn can release associated organic carbon, enhancing microbial priming and mobilization</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-4">In karst soils, tillage-induced breakdown of aggregates and mineralization of organic matter increase CO2 production, promoting carbonate dissolution and Ca2+ leaching; Ca2+ in leachate correlates with losses of organic carbon and nitrogen</cite>.

Management and mitigation: materials and hydrology
- Amendments can reduce cumulative DOC losses. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Across treatments in a calcareous sandy soil under vinasse, cumulative DOC leaching declined over time and was reduced in the order bone char > wood chips biochar > zeolite compared to control, with kinetic parameters quantified by first-order models</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-2">In the broader field, grassland and cropland systems exhibit substantial leaching losses that represent notable fractions of net exchange, underscoring the potential of management to curb off-site carbon loss</cite>.
- Hydrologic retention and structure. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Tillage increased the volume of water leaching and was linked to loss of granular organic N and increased N leaching; the mechanism ties to aggregate disruption, enhanced mineralization, and Ca2+ release, illustrating how soil structure and hydrology jointly govern C and N losses</cite>. Practical implications include minimizing disturbance to macroaggregates, enhancing organic binding, and using hydrologically sorptive minerals to adsorb DOC.

Cryotic leaching and permafrost thaw
- Permafrost soils contain vast carbon stocks that become vulnerable as ground thaws and hydrology and redox conditions shift. <cite id="c62fbfeb-0">Permafrost soils store large carbon pools; thaw exposes organic matter to decomposition, with strong feedbacks where warming accelerates thaw and C emissions</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Arctic permafrost temperatures have risen rapidly, exposing substantial organic carbon to microbial decomposition; global permafrost C (∼50% of soil C) may decline by 30–40% by 2100, with CO2 dominant under aerobic conditions and CH4 under anaerobic conditions</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-2">On the Tibetan Plateau, permafrost soils store ∼160 Pg C; active layer deepening could make 1.07–2.60 Pg C (RCP4.5) or 2.87–5.30 Pg C (RCP8.5) vulnerable to microbial decomposition by century’s end, potentially offsetting regional sinks</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-3">Permafrost contains ∼1035 Pg C in the top 3 m and 272 Pg C below; as soils thaw, emissions of CO2 and CH4 increase, strengthening positive climate feedbacks, with large uncertainties in magnitude and timing</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">Field evidence shows permafrost disturbances are CO2 sources during the growing season, with potential methane release under anaerobic or wetter conditions and carbonate dissolution contributing CO2; deeper active layers and more frequent disturbances increase carbon losses</cite>.

Riverine/erosional export and “old” soil carbon
- Leaching contributes to carbon aging and export. <cite id="29bff118-2">Leached carbon from soils is a main source of dissolved organic and inorganic matter to inland waters, linking terrestrial leaching to aquatic carbon cycling</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-2">In particular, sporadic high precipitation events in arid and semiarid regions preferentially mobilize soil inorganic carbon, which can be transported via runoff and erosion to aquatic systems</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">Dissolution of carbonates and weathering releases inorganic carbon as CO2, and increased soil moisture and ventilation can enhance aquatic CO2 fluxes from disturbed permafrost landscapes</cite>. Together with organic leaching, these processes export “old” soil carbon that, once respired in aquatic or atmospheric systems, yields additional greenhouse gas emissions.

Implications for carbon budgets and practice
- Relative contributions and context. <cite id="29bff118-2">Leaching of SOC in Europe ranges 15–32 g C m−2 yr−1 and can be 4–14% of NEE depending on biome</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-3">In a simulated tropical rainfall Ultisol, leaching was 1.4% of added C while respiration was 10.4%, highlighting that both pathways operate simultaneously and that texture and climate regime modulate their balance</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-0">Because MAOC dominates SOC, protecting mineral associations and reducing mineral dissolution are central to long-term SOC retention</cite>.
- Management levers with evidence. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Biochars and certain mineral amendments reduce cumulative DOC leaching in sandy agroecosystems</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Reducing tillage disturbance to macroaggregates and leveraging Ca2+-rich minerals’ sorptive capacity can lower leaching, while over-intensive tillage increases leaching via enhanced mineralization and Ca2+ mobilization</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-4">Hydrologically, deeper profiles and longer-duration leaching increase losses from upper layers, whereas adsorption in lower horizons can attenuate downstream flux</cite>.
- Uncertainties and research needs. <cite id="29bff118-2">Despite importance, leaching is poorly constrained in many soil carbon budgets and comparisons to respiration remain data-limited</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-1">Mobilization of MAOC depends sensitively on organic ligands, redox chemistry, and microbial communities, with mechanisms that are context-dependent</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Modeling and field projections for permafrost carbon losses vary widely due to uncertainties in microbial functions, moisture, and soil thaw dynamics</cite>. Quantifying how much leached DOC ages carbon in receiving waters and how much of that DOC ultimately respires vs. is buried remains a key gap.

Practical checklist for reducing leaching carbon loss
- Enhance sorption and stabilization: use biochar/bone char amendments to adsorb DOC and foster MAOC formation; manage mineralogy to favor Fe/Al oxides and clay protection. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Bone char and biochar reduced cumulative DOC leaching in a sandy soil</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-0">Fe/Al oxides and clays protect carbon, with MAOC persisting under strong oxidation</cite>.
- Protect soil structure: minimize tillage that fragments macroaggregates and exposes organics; maintain organic binding to reduce N and C losses with runoff. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Tillage increased leaching volume and organic N loss; aggregate disruption and Ca2+ release facilitated mineralization and leaching</cite>.
- Manage hydrology: increase on-site retention (contouring, cover crops), shorten wetting durations, and buffer leachate with riparian sorptive zones. <cite id="29bff118-4">DOC leachate declines with time and increases with depth; early losses from upper layers can be mitigated by structural and hydrologic retention</cite>.
- In cold regions, curb thaw: avoid surface compaction/waterlogging that accelerates active layer deepening; monitor thermokarst development. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Thaw accelerates microbial decomposition and CO2/CH4 emissions</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">Carbonate dissolution and increased ventilation enhance CO2 losses with deeper active layers and more frequent disturbances</cite>.

Summary
- Leaching is a significant and often underestimated pathway of carbon loss, comparable to a few percent of net ecosystem exchange in many ecosystems and sensitive to hydrology, mineralogy, and biology. <cite id="29bff118-2">Forest, grassland, and cropland systems lose 15–32 g C m−2 yr−1 via leaching, representing 4–14% of NEE in Europe</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-3">In laboratory rainfall simulations, leaching was 1.4% of added carbon while respiration was 10.4%, with texture and regime modulating the balance</cite>.
- Protecting and rebuilding mineral associations, using sorptive amendments, and preserving macroaggregates reduce leaching losses, while intensified disturbance and runoff increase them. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Biochar and bone char curbed DOC leaching and altered kinetics</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Aggregate disruption and mineral dissolution amplify losses</cite>.
- In permafrost regions, thaw-driven leaching and decomposition constitute a large positive climate feedback, with projected Pg-scale emissions as protections weaken and hydrology shifts. <cite id="c62fbfeb-0">Thaw exposes stored carbon to decomposition and greenhouse gas emissions</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-2">Pg-scale vulnerabilities emerge as active layers deepen</cite>.

Actionable takeaways
- For croplands and pastures, pair sorptive amendments (biochar/fe/al-rich minerals) with structural conservation (reduced tillage, cover crops) to lower DOC and nutrient losses and rebuild MAOC-like stabilization. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Amendments reduced cumulative DOC leaching</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Aggregate protection reduces mineralization and Ca2+-mediated leaching</cite>.
- In cold regions, prioritize thermal and hydrologic protection of permafrost margins to slow active layer deepening and limit both leaching and decomposition of MAOC-like pools. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Rising temperatures and thaw accelerate microbial decomposition</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">Carbonate dissolution and ventilation increase CO2 fluxes with disturbance</cite>.
- Across systems, quantify leaching budgets and track carbon aging in receiving waters to connect leaching fluxes to ultimate greenhouse gas emissions. <cite id="29bff118-2">Leaching supplies dissolved organic and inorganic matter to inland waters</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">CO2 and CH4 are released once leached carbon reaches anaerobic or aquatic zones</cite>.

Limitations and uncertainties
- Direct, site-specific measurements of leaching versus respiration remain sparse, especially outside forests and managed croplands. <cite id="29bff118-2">Leaching is relatively poorly constrained despite ecosystem importance</cite>.
- Predictions of MAOC mobilization hinge on organism-mediated mineral dissolution and ligand availability, which vary by soil type and vegetation. <cite id="faaccd23-1">Organic ligands, exudates, and redox reactions can transform protected carbon into labile pools</cite>.
- Permafrost carbon projections vary widely with moisture and microbial function, underscoring the need for integrated process-based models and field validation. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Modeling and empirical predictions differ due to uncertainties in microbial functions and environmental drivers</cite>.

Snippet: Soil Organic Carbon Losses: The Balance between Respiration and Leaching, and Phosphorus Mobility in Lateritic Soils (FH Noor): Organic matter (OM) application may contribute to managing lateritic soils by improving aspects of physical, chemical, and biological fertility.  However, the finite persistence of organic carbon (OC), the main component of soil organic matter (SOM), may limit the usefulness of OM addition because decomposition and C leaching promotes C loss from the soil, especially in tropical regions.  The main objectives of this study were to determine the balance and dynamics of soil OC (SOC) due to mineralisation and leaching processes and the relationship of these processes to P mobility in soil.  Two lateritic soils of Western Australia were used.  Both soils were packed into plastic columns and water was added to simulate two rainfall regimes: tropical (4,000 mm year 1) and subtropical (900 mm year 1).  Three types of OM (peat, wheat straw, and lucerne hay) were added at the equivalent of 80Mg ha 1.  Soils were watered weekly to supply one year’s rainfall over a period of six months.  Carbon loss from leaching contributed 1.4% of the total C, whilst respiration accounted for 10.4%.  The Ultisol with a sandy texture had more C loss in leachate than the Oxisol with higher clay content, for the simulated tropical rainfall.  The subtropical rainfall regime resulted in more respiration than the tropical rainfall regime.  Downward movement of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) changed the distribution of non-extractable phosphorus (NP) and bicarbonate phosphorus (BP) in the leaching column, as well as the dislocation of extractable Al and Fe.

Title: Permafrost soils and carbon cycling
Snippet: Because of the large carbon stocks, there are increasing concerns about the potential release of significant amounts of this carbon as greenhouse gases, especially for methane with its greater warming potential compared to carbon dioxide (McGuire et al., 2009;Schuur et al., 2011). The release of carbon may be exacerbated by a strong positive feedback loop where rising soil temperatures and accelerated permafrost degradation lead to increased decomposition of stored organic matter (Oechel et al., 1993;Koven et al., 2011;Harden et al., 2012). However, once permafrost thaws there are radical changes in hydrology, soil conditions, and vegetation communities that create substantial uncertainty as to how quickly and in what direction the thawing of permafrost soils will affect soil carbon balance, greenhouse gas emissions, and climate change (McGuire et al., 2009;Olefeldt et al., 2013;Jorgenson et al., 2013;Walter Anthony et al., 2014). 

In this review, we highlight and discuss important factors affecting the patterns, processes, and carbon stocks of permafrost soils, and summarize recent research developments. In Sect. 2 on permafrost characteristics and transformations, we discuss the formation and distribution of permafrost, effects of cryogenesis on cryostructure patterns, the importance of periglacial freeze-thaw processes on patterned ground, and the consequences of thermokarst landforms resulting from degrading permafrost. In Sect. 3 on cryopedogenesis, we review how biochemical processes are affected by low temperatures, how soil structures differ in the active layer compared to the upper permafrost, and the classification of permafrost soils. In Sects. 4-6 on organic carbon in permafrost soils, we examine permafrost-related factors affecting soil organic carbon (SOC) accumulation, the quantity of organic carbon held in permafrost soils, and its quality and decomposability. Finally, in Sect. 7, we review recent research on the emerging role of permafrost soils in climatic change.
</snippet>

Title: Genomic insights into redox-driven microbial processes for carbon decomposition in thawing Arctic soils and permafrost
Snippet: T emperatures in the Arctic permafrost zone have risen 0.6°C per decade over the last 30 years, twice as fast as the global average (1). As a consequence, the nearsurface permafrost has been thawing and exposing substantial quantities of organic carbon (C) to accelerated decomposition by soil microbes. It is estimated that the permafrost C stock, which contains about 50% of the global soil C (2, 3), will decline 30%-40% by the end of the 21st century (4). This anticipated decline is largely due to stimulated microbial decomposition of the organic C currently stored in permafrost (5). Under aerobic conditions, organic C can be mineralized by soil microorganisms to produce carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), whereas under anaerobic conditions methane (CH 4 ), production can be the dominant C emission pathway in addition to C loss as CO 2 via anaerobic respiration/fermentation (6). Methane, accounting for approximately 2.3% of the expected C loss from thawed permafrost, may be oxidized by CH 4 -oxidizing bacteria before reaching the atmosphere. In addition, sporadic emissions of another potent greenhouse gas (GHG), nitrous oxide, can occur from thawing permafrost due to denitrification (7)(8)(9). Predicting C loss from the Arctic regions, however, has a high level of uncertainty (i.e., ranging from a net C sink to a strong source) (4,10,11), in part due to the poorly understood and complex microbial functions that drive soil C-cycling during permafrost thaw (12). 

Describing soil C dynamics in a warming climate requires understanding how soil microorganisms degrade organic C upon permafrost thaw (13,14). Post-thaw soil moisture varies with topography, leading to the development of both well-drained and inundated areas within the same location (5).

This is likely the main reason for the projected soil organic carbon losses on the TP (Crowther et al., 2016). Below is a synthesis of what “leaching carbon loss” means across ecosystems, with mechanisms, magnitudes, controls, and mitigation options grounded in current evidence.

Definitions and pathways
- Leaching carbon loss refers to the transfer of organic carbon (primarily dissolved organic carbon, DOC) and, in some systems, inorganic carbon (e.g., carbonates) from soils or sediments into water via soil solution, where it can be transported off-site and ultimately respired to CO2 or emitted as methane (CH4) in anaerobic conditions. <cite id="29bff118-2">Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-4">DOC is a mobile soil carbon pool that can be adsorbed, retained, or transported by soil water into the water column</cite>.
- Mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC/MAOM) forms relatively stable associations with clays and iron oxides, but dissolution of minerals or changes in mineral chemistry can mobilize this carbon into more labile, leachable forms. <cite id="faaccd23-0">Mineral-associated organic carbon can constitute up to about 81% of bulk soil organic carbon, with protection by clays and Fe oxides enhancing stability</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-1">Dissolution of minerals by organic ligands (e.g., oxalic acid), root exudates, and reductive dissolution of Fe/Mn can transform mineral-associated organic carbon to accessible forms, priming microbial decomposition and release into solution</cite>.

Magnitude of leaching losses and system controls
- Quantitatively, leaching can rival a nontrivial fraction of net ecosystem carbon exchange in many ecosystems. <cite id="29bff118-2">Soil carbon leached from forests, grasslands, and croplands across Europe was estimated at 15.1, 32.4, and 20.5 g C m−2 yr−1, corresponding to 4%, 14%, and 8% of net ecosystem exchange, respectively</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-2">In arid and semiarid regions, soil inorganic carbon is particularly prone to leaching during sporadic high precipitation events</cite>.
- Hydrology and storm events are key triggers. <cite id="29bff118-2">Very little detailed data exists to compare respiration and leaching, yet extreme precipitation can enhance both, with leaching especially important under episodic wetting in drier regions</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-3">In a lateritic Ultisol under tropical rainfall simulated in columns, leaching accounted for 1.4% of added carbon while respiration accounted for 10.4%, with sandy texture increasing leachate losses; a subtropical regime favored respiration</cite>.
- Depth, adsorption, and time dependence shape losses. <cite id="29bff118-4">DOC in leachate generally increases with soil depth and declines with leaching time due to adsorption and retention in lower layers; upper layers lose more TOC initially, and retention capacity varies with mineralogy and organic matter quality</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-1">First-order kinetics describe DOC leaching with a characteristic half-life, enabling estimation of remaining leachable C as a function of time</cite>.

Mechanisms: MAOC stability and mobilization
- Protection vs. vulnerability. <cite id="faaccd23-0">Associations with Fe/Al oxides and certain clays confer high stability to mineral-associated organic carbon, with over 36% of mineral-associated carbon persisting under strong chemical oxidation, evidencing protection efficacy</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-1">However, mineral dissolution driven by organic ligands, microbes, and redox reactions can liberate carbon, converting protected pools into more accessible and leachable forms</cite>.
- Chemical and biological levers. <cite id="faaccd23-1">Oxalic acid and other organic ligands can chelate minerals, root exudates can destabilize associations, and reductive dissolution of Fe/Mn can release associated organic carbon, enhancing microbial priming and mobilization</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-4">In karst soils, tillage-induced breakdown of aggregates and mineralization of organic matter increase CO2 production, promoting carbonate dissolution and Ca2+ leaching; Ca2+ in leachate correlates with losses of organic carbon and nitrogen</cite>.

Management and mitigation: materials and hydrology
- Amendments can reduce cumulative DOC losses. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Across treatments in a calcareous sandy soil under vinasse, cumulative DOC leaching declined over time and was reduced in the order bone char > wood chips biochar > zeolite compared to control, with kinetic parameters quantified by first-order models</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-2">In the broader field, grassland and cropland systems exhibit substantial leaching losses that represent notable fractions of net exchange, underscoring the potential of management to curb off-site carbon loss</cite>.
- Hydrologic retention and structure. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Tillage increased the volume of water leaching and was linked to loss of granular organic N and increased N leaching; the mechanism ties to aggregate disruption, enhanced mineralization, and Ca2+ release, illustrating how soil structure and hydrology jointly govern C and N losses</cite>. Practical implications include minimizing disturbance to macroaggregates, enhancing organic binding, and using hydrologically sorptive minerals to adsorb DOC.

Cryotic leaching and permafrost thaw
- Permafrost soils contain vast carbon stocks that become vulnerable as ground thaws and hydrology and redox conditions shift. <cite id="c62fbfeb-0">Permafrost soils store large carbon pools; thaw exposes organic matter to decomposition, with strong feedbacks where warming accelerates thaw and C emissions</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Arctic permafrost temperatures have risen rapidly, exposing substantial organic carbon to microbial decomposition; global permafrost C (∼50% of soil C) may decline by 30–40% by 2100, with CO2 dominant under aerobic conditions and CH4 under anaerobic conditions</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-2">On the Tibetan Plateau, permafrost soils store ∼160 Pg C; active layer deepening could make 1.07–2.60 Pg C (RCP4.5) or 2.87–5.30 Pg C (RCP8.5) vulnerable to microbial decomposition by century’s end, potentially offsetting regional sinks</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-3">Permafrost contains ∼1035 Pg C in the top 3 m and 272 Pg C below; as soils thaw, emissions of CO2 and CH4 increase, strengthening positive climate feedbacks, with large uncertainties in magnitude and timing</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">Field evidence shows permafrost disturbances are CO2 sources during the growing season, with potential methane release under anaerobic or wetter conditions and carbonate dissolution contributing CO2; deeper active layers and more frequent disturbances increase carbon losses</cite>.

Riverine/erosional export and “old” soil carbon
- Leaching contributes to carbon aging and export. <cite id="29bff118-2">Leached carbon from soils is a main source of dissolved organic and inorganic matter to inland waters, linking terrestrial leaching to aquatic carbon cycling</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-2">In particular, sporadic high precipitation events in arid and semiarid regions preferentially mobilize soil inorganic carbon, which can be transported via runoff and erosion to aquatic systems</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">Dissolution of carbonates and weathering releases inorganic carbon as CO2, and increased soil moisture and ventilation can enhance aquatic CO2 fluxes from disturbed permafrost landscapes</cite>. Together with organic leaching, these processes export “old” soil carbon that, once respired in aquatic or atmospheric systems, yields additional greenhouse gas emissions.

Implications for carbon budgets and practice
- Relative contributions and context. <cite id="29bff118-2">Leaching of SOC in Europe ranges 15–32 g C m−2 yr−1 and can be 4–14% of NEE depending on biome</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-3">In a simulated tropical rainfall Ultisol, leaching was 1.4% of added C while respiration was 10.4%, highlighting that both pathways operate simultaneously and that texture and climate regime modulate their balance</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-0">Because MAOC dominates SOC, protecting mineral associations and reducing mineral dissolution are central to long-term SOC retention</cite>.
- Management levers with evidence. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Biochars and certain mineral amendments reduce cumulative DOC leaching in sandy agroecosystems</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Reducing tillage disturbance to macroaggregates and leveraging Ca2+-rich minerals’ sorptive capacity can lower leaching, while over-intensive tillage increases leaching via enhanced mineralization and Ca2+ mobilization</cite>. <cite id="29bff118-4">Hydrologically, deeper profiles and longer-duration leaching increase losses from upper layers, whereas adsorption in lower horizons can attenuate downstream flux</cite>.
- Uncertainties and research needs. <cite id="29bff118-2">Despite importance, leaching is poorly constrained in many soil carbon budgets and comparisons to respiration remain data-limited</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-1">Mobilization of MAOC depends sensitively on organic ligands, redox chemistry, and microbial communities, with mechanisms that are context-dependent</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Modeling and field projections for permafrost carbon losses vary widely due to uncertainties in microbial functions, moisture, and soil thaw dynamics</cite>. Quantifying how much leached DOC ages carbon in receiving waters and how much of that DOC ultimately respires vs. is buried remains a key gap.

Practical checklist for reducing leaching carbon loss
- Enhance sorption and stabilization: use biochar/bone char amendments to adsorb DOC and foster MAOC formation; manage mineralogy to favor Fe/Al oxides and clay protection. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Bone char and biochar reduced cumulative DOC leaching in a sandy soil</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-0">Fe/Al oxides and clays protect carbon, with MAOC persisting under strong oxidation</cite>.
- Protect soil structure: minimize tillage that fragments macroaggregates and exposes organics; maintain organic binding to reduce N and C losses with runoff. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Tillage increased leaching volume and organic N loss; aggregate disruption and Ca2+ release facilitated mineralization and leaching</cite>.
- Manage hydrology: increase on-site retention (contouring, cover crops), shorten wetting durations, and buffer leachate with riparian sorptive zones. <cite id="29bff118-4">DOC leachate declines with time and increases with depth; early losses from upper layers can be mitigated by structural and hydrologic retention</cite>.
- In cold regions, curb thaw: avoid surface compaction/waterlogging that accelerates active layer deepening; monitor thermokarst development. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Thaw accelerates microbial decomposition and CO2/CH4 emissions</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">Carbonate dissolution and increased ventilation enhance CO2 losses with deeper active layers and more frequent disturbances</cite>.

Summary
- Leaching is a significant and often underestimated pathway of carbon loss, comparable to a few percent of net ecosystem exchange in many ecosystems and sensitive to hydrology, mineralogy, and biology. <cite id="29bff118-2">Forest, grassland, and cropland systems lose 15–32 g C m−2 yr−1 via leaching, representing 4–14% of NEE in Europe</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-3">In laboratory rainfall simulations, leaching was 1.4% of added carbon while respiration was 10.4%, with texture and regime modulating the balance</cite>.
- Protecting and rebuilding mineral associations, using sorptive amendments, and preserving macroaggregates reduce leaching losses, while intensified disturbance and runoff increase them. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Biochar and bone char curbed DOC leaching and altered kinetics</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Aggregate disruption and mineral dissolution amplify losses</cite>.
- In permafrost regions, thaw-driven leaching and decomposition constitute a large positive climate feedback, with projected Pg-scale emissions as protections weaken and hydrology shifts. <cite id="c62fbfeb-0">Thaw exposes stored carbon to decomposition and greenhouse gas emissions</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-2">Pg-scale vulnerabilities emerge as active layers deepen</cite>.

Actionable takeaways
- For croplands and pastures, pair sorptive amendments (biochar/fe/al-rich minerals) with structural conservation (reduced tillage, cover crops) to lower DOC and nutrient losses and rebuild MAOC-like stabilization. <cite id="faaccd23-2">Amendments reduced cumulative DOC leaching</cite>. <cite id="faaccd23-4">Aggregate protection reduces mineralization and Ca2+-mediated leaching</cite>.
- In cold regions, prioritize thermal and hydrologic protection of permafrost margins to slow active layer deepening and limit both leaching and decomposition of MAOC-like pools. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Rising temperatures and thaw accelerate microbial decomposition</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">Carbonate dissolution and ventilation increase CO2 fluxes with disturbance</cite>.
- Across systems, quantify leaching budgets and track carbon aging in receiving waters to connect leaching fluxes to ultimate greenhouse gas emissions. <cite id="29bff118-2">Leaching supplies dissolved organic and inorganic matter to inland waters</cite>. <cite id="c62fbfeb-4">CO2 and CH4 are released once leached carbon reaches anaerobic or aquatic zones</cite>.

Limitations and uncertainties
- Direct, site-specific measurements of leaching versus respiration remain sparse, especially outside forests and managed croplands. <cite id="29bff118-2">Leaching is relatively poorly constrained despite ecosystem importance</cite>.
- Predictions of MAOC mobilization hinge on organism-mediated mineral dissolution and ligand availability, which vary by soil type and vegetation. <cite id="faaccd23-1">Organic ligands, exudates, and redox reactions can transform protected carbon into labile pools</cite>.
- Permafrost carbon projections vary widely with moisture and microbial function, underscoring the need for integrated process-based models and field validation. <cite id="c62fbfeb-1">Modeling and empirical predictions differ due to uncertainties in microbial functions and environmental drivers</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Soil dissolved organic carbon leaching characteristics of the coastal saline seepweed wetlands in the Wuleidaowan national wetland
Snippet: As the most active component of soil TOC (Total Organic Carbon), DOC (Dissolved Organic Carbon) is either adsorbed by the soil and used by plants or transported by soil water into the water column, where it participates in the broader carbon cycle. As a substantial "mobile carbon pool" in soils, its leaching process is an essential pathway for the loss of soil TOC. This paper analysed the investigated the leaching characteristics of soil DOC by simulating leaching in an indoor soil column based on the spatial distribution of soil TOC and DOC contents in order to reveal the leaching and migration characteristics of soil DOC at different depths and its main influencing factors. The DOC content of soil leachate varies somewhat under conditions such as PH and soil phosphorous content. However, the overall trend is that the DOC content of soil leachate generally increases with the depth of the soil layer. The DOC content in the soil leachate gradually decreased with increasing leaching time. In the absence of exogenous carbon recharge, the loss of TOC from the upper layers of the soil was significantly more remarkable due to the prolonged leaching. In addition, soil TOC loss declined after leaching and decreased significantly with increasing soil depth. Because the soil DOC is adsorbed and trapped in other layers during leaching, the DOC in the upper layer was always lost during the leaching test. The experiments used highly concentrated DOC solutions as drench solutions. According to the analysis of the intensity of the fluorescence centres of each soil layer in the three-dimensional fluorescence pattern of the drench solution of each soil layer, the ability of different soil layers to adsorb and retain organic matter of different fractions differs. In addition, the selected soil layers planted with Saline seepweed show a general decreasing trend in the ability to adsorb and retain organic matter as the depth increases.

snippet.text: As the most active component of soil TOC (Total Organic Carbon), DOC (Dissolved Organic Carbon) is either adsorbed by the soil and used by plants or transported by soil water into the water column, where it participates in the broader carbon cycle. As a substantial "mobile carbon pool" in soils, its leaching process is an essential pathway for the loss of soil TOC. This paper analysed the investigated the leaching characteristics of soil DOC by simulating leaching in an indoor soil column based on the spatial distribution of soil TOC and DOC contents in order to reveal the leaching and migration characteristics of soil DOC at different depths and its main influencing factors. The DOC content of soil leachate varies somewhat under conditions such as PH and soil phosphorous content. However, the overall trend is that the DOC content of soil leachate generally increases with the depth of the soil layer. The DOC content in the soil leachate gradually decreased with increasing leaching time. In the absence of exogenous carbon recharge, the loss of TOC from the upper layers of the soil was significantly more remarkable due to the prolonged leaching. In addition, soil TOC loss declined after leaching and decreased significantly with increasing soil depth. Because the soil DOC is adsorbed and trapped in other layers during leaching, the DOC in the upper layer was always lost during the leaching test. The experiments used highly concentrated DOC solutions as drench solutions. According to the analysis of the intensity of the fluorescence centres of each soil layer in the three-dimensional fluorescence pattern of the drench solution of each soil layer, the ability of different soil layers to adsorb and retain organic matter of different fractions differs. In addition, the selected soil layers planted with Saline seepweed show a general decreasing trend in the ability to adsorb and retain organic matter as the depth increases.

documents.title: Comparing soil carbon loss through respiration and leaching under extreme precipitation events in arid and semiarid grasslands
documents.snippet:
Soils store approximately 2500 Pg of carbon (including organic and inorganic carbon) globally, equivalent to 3.3 and 4.5 times the carbon in the atmosphere (760 Pg) and terrestrial plants (560 Pg), respectively (Lal, 2004). Slight variations in the soil carbon pool will hence severely influence atmospheric CO 2 concentrations and have important implications for climate change (Davidson and Janssens, 2006;Trumbore and Czimczik, 2008). Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss. While respiration has received considerable research attention (Raich and Schlesinger, 1992;Raich and Potter, 1995;Hoover et al., 2016;Burri et al., 2015;Escolar et al., 2015), leaching is relatively poorly constrained despite its importance in certain ecosystems (Cole et al., 2007;Battin et al., 2008;Liu et al., 2017). For instance, soil carbon leached from forests, grasslands, and croplands is estimated to be 15.1, 32.4, and 20.5 g C m −2 yr −1 across Europe, representing 4, 14, and 8 % of net ecosystem exchange (NEE), respectively (Kindler et al., 2011). Additionally, leaching of carbon previously preserved in surface litter and soil layers is believed to be a main source of dissolved organic and inorganic matter Published by Copernicus Publications on behalf of the European Geosciences Union. 

T. Liu et al.: Comparing soil carbon loss through respiration in inland waters (Spencer et al., 2008). In particular, soil inorganic carbon (SIC) that occurs widely in arid and semiarid regions is more prone to leaching than organic carbon during sporadic high precipitation events (Lal and Kimble, 2000). Despite the importance of leaching loss in regional soil carbon budgets, very little detailed data exists to investigate and compare the relative contribution of respiration and leaching processes to soil carbon loss.

Title: Mineral-mediated stability of organic carbon in soil and relevant interaction mechanisms
Snippet: Soil samples collected from nine sites with different clay and iron oxide content are selected to evaluate the interaction among clay minerals, iron oxides, and organic carbon, as well as the organic carbon stability in the Eastern Usambara Mountains [292].Mineral-associated organic carbon accounts for up to 81% of the bulk organic carbon in the soil environment, and the larger amount of mineral-associated organic carbon persists in soil due to the soil weathering with decreasing aluminous clay (kaolinite, gibbsite) to Fe oxide (goethite, hematite) ratio.Iron oxides act as the binding sites to combine negative clay minerals and organic carbon, forming mineral-associated organic carbon with high stability against chemical or biological degradation.Over 36% of organic carbon associated with the soil minerals can be preserved even after a strong chemical oxidation process, evidencing its high stability and protection efficacy on the soil minerals.

Title: Mineral-mediated stability of organic carbon in soil and relevant interaction mechanisms
Snippet: While the formed mineral-organic carbon association stabilizes carbon, the dissolution of minerals by organic carbon might lead to its destruction, thus causing the mobilization of organic carbon.Organic ligands, such as oxalic acid released from plant roots, can serve as the chelating moiety to dissolve the short-ranged minerals [186,252].This process will result in the transformation of mineral-associated organic carbon to accessible organic carbon, potentially causing a priming impact with soil microorganisms [17,252,253].In addition to organic ligands, other root exudates can destabilize the mineral-organic carbon associated with the support of microorganisms [253,254].Reductive dissolution of Fe or Mn minerals by organic carbon, with or without microorganisms, has been reported, which will cause the release of associated organic carbon [255].

Title: Soil Organic Carbon Losses: The Balance between Respiration and Leaching, and Phosphorus Mobility in Lateritic Soils
Snippet: Soil Organic Carbon Losses: The Balance between Respiration and Leaching, and Phosphorus Mobility in Lateritic Soils (FH Noor): Organic matter (OM) application may contribute to managing lateritic soils by improving aspects of physical, chemical, and biological fertility.  However, the finite persistence of organic carbon (OC), the main component of soil organic matter (SOM), may limit the usefulness of OM addition because decomposition and C leaching promotes C loss from the soil, especially in tropical regions.  The main objectives of this study were to determine the balance and dynamics of soil OC (SOC) due to mineralisation and leaching processes and the relationship of these processes to P mobility in soil.  Two lateritic soils of Western Australia were used.  Both soils were packed into plastic columns and water was added to simulate two rainfall regimes: tropical (4,000 mm year 1) and subtropical (900 mm year 1).  Three types of OM (peat, wheat straw, and lucerne hay) were added at the equivalent of 80Mg ha 1.  Soils were watered weekly to supply one year’s rainfall over a period of six months.  Carbon loss from leaching contributed 1.4% of the total C, whilst respiration accounted for 10.4%.  The Ultisol with a sandy texture had more C loss in leachate than the Oxisol with higher clay content, for the simulated tropical rainfall.  The subtropical rainfall regime resulted in more respiration than the tropical rainfall regime.  Downward movement of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) changed the distribution of non-extractable phosphorus (NP) and bicarbonate phosphorus (BP) in the leaching column, as well as the dislocation of extractable Al and Fe.

Title: Tillage-Induced Fragmentation of Large Soil Macroaggregates Increases Nitrogen Leaching in a Subtropical Karst Region
Snippet: Zhang et al. [13] found higher amounts of N in leachate collected in the subsoil were associated with less soluble N in the upper soil, which is consistent with our result. In addition, there was a significant negative correlation between sand content and nitrogen leaching in our study, which is contrary to the result of Beaudoin et al. [40]. They found that higher soil sand content was associated with greater N leaching. The saturated water conductivity of sandy soil is high, and as more water passes through a unit area in a unit time, more dissolved N can be transported. However, tillage treatments (T2, T3, and T4) with lower sand content led to a greater annual volume of water leaching compared with CK (T0) in our study (Figure S1). We speculated that it was the crushing of large particles in the soil texture caused by tillage [41] that resulted in the loss of granular organic N and increased amounts of N leaching. 

There was no significant relationship between exchangeable Ca in soil and N in leachate in our study. However, interestingly, there was a significant correlation between the content of Ca in leachate and the amount of leached nitrogen (Figure S2). In a previous study, it was found that Ca 2+ in the leaching solution was significantly correlated with the loss of organic carbon [22]. Organic carbon and nitrogen are the main components of organic matter. In karst areas, the soil is rich in carbonate (such as calcium carbonate), and its reprecipitation can reduce the utilization of organic matter in the aggregates by microorganisms and promote the accumulation of soil organic matter [42]. However, the mineralization of soil organic matter under tillage resulted in the increase in CO 2 , which promoted the dissolution of carbonate and the leaching of Ca 2+ . This eventually resulted in a significant correlation between Ca 2+ in leached solution and leached N.

Title: Permafrost soils and carbon cycling
Snippet: Because of the large carbon stocks, there are increasing concerns about the potential release of significant amounts of this carbon as greenhouse gases, especially for methane with its greater warming potential compared to carbon dioxide (McGuire et al., 2009;Schuur et al., 2011). The release of carbon may be exacerbated by a strong positive feedback loop where rising soil temperatures and accelerated permafrost degradation lead to increased decomposition of stored organic matter (Oechel et al., 1993;Koven et al., 2011;Harden et al., 2012). However, once permafrost thaws there are radical changes in hydrology, soil conditions, and vegetation communities that create substantial uncertainty as to how quickly and in what direction the thawing of permafrost soils will affect soil carbon balance, greenhouse gas emissions, and climate change (McGuire et al., 2009;Olefeldt et al., 2013;Jorgenson et al., 2013;Walter Anthony et al., 2014). 

In this review, we highlight and discuss important factors affecting the patterns, processes, and carbon stocks of permafrost soils, and summarize recent research developments. In Sect. 2 on permafrost characteristics and transformations, we discuss the formation and distribution of permafrost, effects of cryogenesis on cryostructure patterns, the importance of periglacial freeze-thaw processes on patterned ground, and the consequences of thermokarst landforms resulting from degrading permafrost. In Sect. 3 on cryopedogenesis, we review how biochemical processes are affected by low temperatures, how soil structures differ in the active layer compared to the upper permafrost, and the classification of permafrost soils. In Sects. 4-6 on organic carbon in permafrost soils, we examine permafrost-related factors affecting soil organic carbon (SOC) accumulation, the quantity of organic carbon held in permafrost soils, and its quality and decomposability. Finally, in Sect. 7, we review recent research on the emerging role of permafrost soils in climatic change.

Title: Genomic insights into redox-driven microbial processes for carbon decomposition in thawing Arctic soils and permafrost
Snippet: T emperatures in the Arctic permafrost zone have risen 0.6°C per decade over the last 30 years, twice as fast as the global average (1). As a consequence, the nearsurface permafrost has been thawing and exposing substantial quantities of organic carbon (C) to accelerated decomposition by soil microbes. It is estimated that the permafrost C stock, which contains about 50% of the global soil C (2, 3), will decline 30%-40% by the end of the 21st century (4). This anticipated decline is largely due to stimulated microbial decomposition of the organic C currently stored in permafrost (5). Under aerobic conditions, organic C can be mineralized by soil microorganisms to produce carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), whereas under anaerobic conditions methane (CH 4 ), production can be the dominant C emission pathway in addition to C loss as CO 2 via anaerobic respiration/fermentation (6). Methane, accounting for approximately 2.3% of the expected C loss from thawed permafrost, may be oxidized by CH 4 -oxidizing bacteria before reaching the atmosphere. In addition, sporadic emissions of another potent greenhouse gas (GHG), nitrous oxide, can occur from thawing permafrost due to denitrification (7)(8)(9). Predicting C loss from the Arctic regions, however, has a high level of uncertainty (i.e., ranging from a net C sink to a strong source) (4,10,11), in part due to the poorly understood and complex microbial functions that drive soil C-cycling during permafrost thaw (12). 

Describing soil C dynamics in a warming climate requires understanding how soil microorganisms degrade organic C upon permafrost thaw (13,14). Post-thaw soil moisture varies with topography, leading to the development of both well-drained and inundated areas within the same location (5).

Title: Past, present, and future geo-biosphere interactions on the Tibetan Plateau and implications for permafrost
Snippet: In frozen soil, microbial activity is strongly inhibited, leading to organic carbon accumulation (Zimov et al., 2006). According to Mu et al. (2015), permafrost soils of the TP store about 160 +/− 87 Pg C, representing approximately 8.7% of that in the northern circumpolar permafrost region. Thawing of permafrost will release large parts of the carbon into the atmosphere as CO 2 and CH 4 (Schuur et al., 2015). This is likely the main reason for the projected soil organic carbon losses on the TP (Crowther et al., 2016). The gradual permafrost thawing due to active layer deepening is projected to make 1.07 to 2.60 Pg (RCP4.5) or 2.87 to 5.30 Pg (RCP8.5) soil organic carbon vulnerable to microbial decomposition by the end of the century, which could largely offset the regional carbon sink (Wang et al., 2020b). Soil organic carbon losses due to permafrost thaw are projected to be in the range of 15 to 69 Pg until 2020 and up to 3 m soil depth (Mu et al., 2015;Ding et al., 2016;Bosch et al., 2017;Jiang et al., 2019), amounting up to more than one-third of the total soil organic carbon stocks. However, there is significant spatial heterogeneity in the predicted soil organic carbon losses until 2070. Estimates range from <6.5 kg C m − 2 to >24 kg C m − 2 according to RCP2.6 projections (Bosch et al., 2017). This calls for a detailed analysis of possible soil organic carbon losses for different landscape units of the TP and how the feedback mechanisms with vegetation and land use will change.

snippet.text:
Because of the large carbon stocks, there are increasing concerns about the potential release of significant amounts of this carbon as greenhouse gases, especially for methane with its greater warming potential compared to carbon dioxide (McGuire et al., 2009;Schuur et al., 2011). The release of carbon may be exacerbated by a strong positive feedback loop where rising soil temperatures and accelerated permafrost degradation lead to increased decomposition of stored organic matter (Oechel et al., 1993;Koven et al., 2011;Harden et al., 2012). However, once permafrost thaws there are radical changes in hydrology, soil conditions, and vegetation communities that create substantial uncertainty as to how quickly and in what direction the thawing of permafrost soils will affect soil carbon balance, greenhouse gas emissions, and climate change (McGuire et al., 2009;Olefeldt et al., 2013;Jorgenson et al., 2013;Walter Anthony et al., 2014). 

In this review, we highlight and discuss important factors affecting the patterns, processes, and carbon stocks of permafrost soils, and summarize recent research developments. In Sect. 2 on permafrost characteristics and transformations, we discuss the formation and distribution of permafrost, effects of cryogenesis on cryostructure patterns, the importance of periglacial freeze-thaw processes on patterned ground, and the consequences of thermokarst landforms resulting from degrading permafrost. In Sect. 3 on cryopedogenesis, we review how biochemical processes are affected by low temperatures, how soil structures differ in the active layer compared to the upper permafrost, and the classification of permafrost soils. In Sects. 4-6 on organic carbon in permafrost soils, we examine permafrost-related factors affecting soil organic carbon (SOC) accumulation, the quantity of organic carbon held in permafrost soils, and its quality and decomposability. Finally, in Sect. 7, we review recent research on the emerging role of permafrost soils in climatic change.

snippet.text:
T emperatures in the Arctic permafrost zone have risen 0.6°C per decade over the last 30 years, twice as fast as the global average (1). As a consequence, the nearsurface permafrost has been thawing and exposing substantial quantities of organic carbon (C) to accelerated decomposition by soil microbes. It is estimated that the permafrost C stock, which contains about 50% of the global soil C (2, 3), will decline 30%-40% by the end of the 21st century (4). This anticipated decline is largely due to stimulated microbial decomposition of the organic C currently stored in permafrost (5). Under aerobic conditions, organic C can be mineralized by soil microorganisms to produce carbon dioxide (CO 2 ), whereas under anaerobic conditions methane (CH 4 ), production can be the dominant C emission pathway in addition to C loss as CO 2 via anaerobic respiration/fermentation (6). Methane, accounting for approximately 2.3% of the expected C loss from thawed permafrost, may be oxidized by CH 4 -oxidizing bacteria before reaching the atmosphere. In addition, sporadic emissions of another potent greenhouse gas (GHG), nitrous oxide, can occur from thawing permafrost due to denitrification (7)(8)(9). Predicting C loss from the Arctic regions, however, has a high level of uncertainty (i.e., ranging from a net C sink to a strong source) (4,10,11), in part due to the poorly understood and complex microbial functions that drive soil C-cycling during permafrost thaw (12). 

Describing soil C dynamics in a warming climate requires understanding how soil microorganisms degrade organic C upon permafrost thaw (13,14). Post-thaw soil moisture varies with topography, leading to the development of both well-drained and inundated areas within the same location (5).

This calls for a detailed analysis of possible soil organic carbon losses for different landscape units of the TP and how the feedback mechanisms with vegetation and land use will change.

Summary
Leaching of dissolved organic and inorganic carbon (DOC/DIC) from soils to waters is an export pathway that can represent a net carbon loss for terrestrial ecosystems, but its impact is often offset by coupled biogeochemical processes that recycle, retain, or sequester carbon within the soil–water continuum. The net ecosystem outcome depends on the balance among net primary production (NPP), heterotrophic respiration, hydrology-driven export, in-stream mineralization/CO2 evasion, and burial in sediments and coastal systems. Across ecosystems, leaching can account for a measurable fraction of net ecosystem exchange (NEE), sometimes as high as a few to tens of percent, but substantial in-stream processing and episodic hydrologic events can either amplify losses or promote retention and burial, making the system response context-dependent. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss, with leaching representing 4–14% of NEE in forests, grasslands, and croplands across Europe</cite><cite id="b86345ee-3">Isotopic tracking found that 75% of CO2 exiting soil via groundwater mass flow was recent photosynthate, and although this leached carbon was only 2% of annual net carbon fixed, losses could reach ~9% in wetter years</cite><cite id="b86345ee-4">Modeling suggests a historical global terrestrial DOC leaching of ~250 Tg C yr−1 with strong coupling to runoff and NPP</cite>.

What leaching is and its measured magnitudes
Leaching refers to the export of dissolved carbon (organic and inorganic) from soils into groundwater and surface waters via vertical diffusion and preferential flow, and it represents one of two principal soil carbon losses alongside respiratory CO2 release. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss, with leaching particularly important in forests, grasslands, and croplands</cite><cite id="b86345ee-2">Soils lose carbon via surface runoff, channel erosion, lateral drainage, and vertical leaching to groundwaters</cite>. At the ecosystem scale, leaching fluxes are substantial: <cite id="b86345ee-0">across Europe, leaching rates of 15.1, 32.4, and 20.5 g C m−2 yr−1 in forests, grasslands, and croplands corresponded to 4, 14, and 8% of NEE, respectively</cite>. Hydrology and climate modulate these losses: <cite id="b86345ee-3">seasonal drought followed by heavy rains in boreal Finland increased leaching from 7.5 to 15.5 mg L−1, driving a fivefold increase in watershed losses from 1700 to 9400 tonnes C</cite>, and <cite id="b86345ee-4">global simulations show a strong positive correlation between runoff and DOC leaching (R2 = 0.75) and that boreal zones exhibit the largest relative increases due to runoff changes</cite>. <cite id="b86345ee-4">Surface soil layers contribute about 90% of total DOC leaching even though they hold only ~40% of soil DOC stocks, highlighting the importance of shallow soils and preferential flow</cite>.

Fate of leached carbon in the inland and coastal continuum
Once exported, dissolved carbon undergoes extensive processing within rivers, estuaries, and coastal zones. <cite id="dc0e3e74-0">Riverine carbon budgets include in-situ production, consumption, and phase changes; small streams and rivers can exhibit large CO2 evasion due to high DIC and gas transfer velocities, though global quantification remains uncertain</cite>. <cite id="dc0e3e74-1">Rivers both transport and transform carbon: DOC is partly mineralized in-stream to DIC, DIC can be fixed photoautotrophically or exchanged with the atmosphere, and global riverine exports range from 0.17–0.78 Pg DOC yr−1 and 0.38–2.6 Pg DIC yr−1 to the oceans, with a net atmospheric CO2 evasion of 0.26–1.8 Pg C yr−1</cite>. Photodegradation and microbial processing rapidly alter DOC: <cite id="dc0e3e74-2">sunlight oxidizes DOC to CO2 and CO, while in-stream processes (photodegradation, flocculation, microbial consumption) and DIC transformations (degassing, photosynthesis, carbonate reactions) control riverine dissolved carbon dynamics</cite>. Hydrology strongly governs fate: <cite id="dc0e3e74-3">the type and intensity of hydrologic events controls whether DOC is transported conservatively or processed; with increasing discharge, export of millennial-aged terrestrial OC increases, indicating that rivers can deliver aged carbon to the ocean</cite>. At the continental scale, much terrestrial carbon is removed before reaching the ocean: <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">only ~0.95 Pg C yr−1 of a terrestrial export of 5.1 Pg C yr−1 reaches the oceans, with the majority of DOC removed by microbial/photochemical degradation, emitted as CO2 and CH4, or buried in sediments</cite>. Freshwater burial can be significant: <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">global lake, pond, reservoir, and floodplain burial rates are estimated between 0.2–6 Pg C yr−1 (with ~0.6 Pg C yr−1 commonly used), and adsorption to mineral particles followed by settling can direct organic carbon to sediments</cite>.

Do coupled processes offset leaching? Evidence from soils, watersheds, and coasts
Coupled processes can offset, amplify, or redistribute leaching losses, depending on ecosystem carbon balance and hydrologic/chemical conditions. First, within the soil–plant system, productivity and heterotrophic processing modulate whether net carbon accrues despite export. <cite id="b86345ee-3">In a boreal forest, 75% of CO2 exiting soil via groundwater mass flow was recent photosynthate, indicating rapid cycling between atmosphere–soil; although this leached carbon was ~2% of annual net fixation, it could reach ~9% under wetter conditions, demonstrating that export can erode but not necessarily overturn a positive NEP</cite>. Second, hydrologic coupling to groundwater and surface waters can either retain or accelerate loss: <cite id="b86345ee-2">drainage of groundwater enriched in dissolved carbon acts as an important source of CO2 degassing, linking soil leaching to atmospheric CO2</cite>, whereas <cite id="b86345ee-4">higher runoff increases DOC leaching, highlighting transport limitation as a key control</cite>. Third, riverine processing redistributes carbon among pools: <cite id="dc0e3e74-1">DIC originating from soil respiration and weathering is often lost as CO2, while a fraction can be respired, photosynthesized, or buried; net CO2 evasion from rivers to atmosphere is substantial</cite>, and <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">microbial and photochemical degradation typically removes most leached DOC before ocean delivery, with burial occurring when particulate/adsorbed carbon settles</cite>. Thus, leaching is not a one-way loss to the atmosphere; rather, it diverts carbon to fast (days–months) biogeochemical loops in rivers and sediments that can result in CO2 evasion, methane emissions, or storage, partially offsetting soil losses.

Fourth, soil carbon formation and hydrologically coupled redistribution can balance leaching over longer timescales. <cite id="b86345ee-3">Proximity of soil to water increased DOC exiting the soil fivefold, but in some cases this reflected long-term groundwater accumulation rather than recent biological activity, indicating that leaching can mobilize legacy soil carbon pools as well as contemporary production</cite>. <cite id="b86345ee-4">Surface soils contribute most leaching but hold only ~40% of soil DOC stocks; this implies that mineral-protected and deeper pools may remain relatively recalcitrant, while frequent leaching of surface carbon can maintain a dynamic balance between formation and export</cite>. In grasslands, for example, <cite id="b86345ee-4">DOC export was a significant C flux of about 8% of net ecosystem production in an acidic sandy soil, illustrating that export can rival internal sequestration in some systems, whereas in clay-rich soils export was small and not correlated with SOC stocks</cite>. Across climate gradients, <cite id="b86345ee-3">drought–wet year dynamics can increase leaching by concentrating easily leached surface carbon during wet periods, implying that interannual variability in hydrology and productivity controls the degree to which losses offset net gains</cite>. Globally, <cite id="b86345ee-4">leaching increases with both NPP and runoff; temperate and subtropical zones show rising leaching mainly with NPP increase, while boreal zones are most sensitive to runoff, underscoring that productivity-driven inputs and hydrologic transport jointly determine net ecosystem balance</cite>.

Net ecosystem outcome: when is leaching a net loss, and when is it offset?
Taken together, leaching is an export pathway that, when unopposed, represents a net carbon loss from terrestrial ecosystems because it removes carbon from soil and biomass pools to be processed in waters and ultimately released to the atmosphere or buried. However, ecosystem carbon budgets integrate coupled processes that can offset or amplify these losses. In carbon-neutral or carbon-negative ecosystems (e.g., high-latitude forests with strong heterotrophy), leaching can erode limited gains or even represent a net loss as respired CO2 is exported to rivers and released to the atmosphere. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Leaching is 14% of NEE in grasslands and 4% in forests in Europe, indicating that export can rival internal carbon sequestration in some ecosystems</cite><cite id="b86345ee-3">and can rise to ~9% under wetter conditions</cite>. In productive, well-drained upland forests, leaching may be a small fraction of NEP and offset by net inputs and soil formation, but during storms or snowmelt, preferential flow can transiently double or triple losses, making the system behave closer to a net exporter during events. <cite id="b86345ee-4">Transport-limited DOC leaching increases with runoff, and surface soils’ disproportionate contribution to leaching implies that hydrologic connectivity and preferential flow can rapidly shift the balance toward export</cite>.

Conversely, in landscapes with strong lateral retention, burial, or rapid biological processing within the watershed, a portion of leached carbon is reincorporated into biomass, sediments, or coastal storage, offsetting the apparent loss. <cite id="dc0e3e74-1">Rivers both transport and transform DOC/DIC, with in-stream mineralization and photosynthesis re-partitioning carbon within the aquatic system</cite><cite id="dc0e3e74-4">and microbial/photochemical degradation and sediment burial removing terrestrial carbon from further atmospheric exchange</cite>. In agricultural and riparian settings, elevated mineral adsorption and settling can promote burial of DOM–mineral complexes, reducing net atmospheric flux from leaching. <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">Adsorption to mineral particles and subsequent settling can direct dissolved organic matter to sediments, where burial rates in inland waters can be substantial</cite>. These coupled processes mean that “leaching” should be viewed as a flux redistribution rather than a simple one-way loss: carbon is cycled through fast aquatic pathways (CO2 evasion, microbial mineralization) or stored in sediments/coasts, and the net ecosystem effect depends on the balance of inputs (NPP), outputs (leaching, respiration, erosion), and in-system transformations.

Timescales, uncertainties, and system gradients
Short-term (event-to-annual) versus long-term (decadal–centennial) perspectives matter. <cite id="b86345ee-3">Isotope studies show that leached CO2 to groundwater is overwhelmingly recent (annual to sub-annual), indicating rapid coupling of terrestrial productivity to aquatic loss</cite>, while <cite id="dc0e3e74-3">increasing discharge can export millennial-aged terrestrial DOC and particulate organic carbon, showing that legacy soil carbon can also be mobilized and delivered to oceans</cite>. Over longer timescales, burial in inland waters and coastal zones can represent a sink for terrestrial carbon, but global estimates are uncertain due to uneven sampling and strong controls by hydrology, chemistry, and land use. <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">Global freshwater burial rates vary widely (0.2–6 Pg C yr−1), with commonly used values of ~0.6 Pg C yr−1 acknowledging large uncertainty; only a small fraction of terrestrial DOC reaches the ocean because most is transformed within river systems</cite>. Importantly, climate and land-use change can shift the balance toward net loss. <cite id="b86345ee-4">Increases in runoff and NPP both enhance DOC leaching, with boreal regions becoming more loss-prone under increased precipitation/snow and forests potentially losing more during higher summer rainfall</cite>, while in cultivated fields near streams, <cite id="b86345ee-3">leaching risks are elevated due to lower carbon inputs and hydrologic connectivity</cite>.

Practical synthesis for the question
- Leaching is a measurable and often non-negligible export pathway that can act as a net carbon loss when respiratory CO2 and DOC/DIC are delivered to waters and subsequently mineralized or degassed. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Across Europe, leaching is 4–14% of NEE in major land covers</cite><cite id="b86345ee-3">and can reach ~9% in wet years</cite>. 
- However, coupled processes frequently offset this loss: in-stream and photodegradative mineralization redistribute carbon among pools, while burial in sediments and coastal systems sequesters a portion; hydrologic connectivity and residence time modulate whether losses dominate or are retained. <cite id="dc0e3e74-1">Rivers transform and transport carbon, with substantial CO2 evasion and variable burial</cite><cite id="dc0e3e74-4">and microbial/photochemical degradation typically removes most leached DOC before ocean delivery</cite>. 
- Whether leaching represents a net loss or offset depends on the ecosystem’s productivity–respiration balance and hydroclimatic regime. In carbon sinks (e.g., productive forests with low heterotrophy), leaching erodes gains; in degraded or arid systems with low productivity and high hydrologic connectivity, leaching can exceed internal sequestration, acting closer to a net loss; in landscapes with strong burial or rapid watershed cycling, a fraction of leached carbon is reincorporated or stored, attenuating the net loss. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Leaching is particularly important in fragile, low-productivity ecosystems</cite><cite id="b86345ee-4">and its magnitude scales with runoff and NPP</cite><cite id="b86345ee-3">with drought–wet year dynamics amplifying losses via accumulation and mobilization of easily leached carbon</cite>. 
- Thus, the correct framing is “leaching is a net carbon loss only to the extent it is not offset by coupled soil carbon formation, in-system biological processing, lateral redistribution, and burial.” <cite id="b86345ee-3">Proximity of soil to water can increase DOC export fivefold, but this carbon can reflect long-term groundwater accumulation rather than recent productivity, evidencing internal cycling and redistribution</cite><cite id="b86345ee-4">and surface soils’ disproportionate role in leaching implies that mineral protection and hydrologic export jointly determine net ecosystem outcomes</cite>.

Key uncertainties and what would resolve them
Quantifying the net effect requires resolving spatially explicit coupling between productivity, hydrology, and in-stream carbon transformations. <cite id="dc0e3e74-0">Uncertainties in riverine carbon budgets stem from incomplete knowledge of in-situ production, consumption, and phase changes, with small streams contributing disproportionately to CO2 evasion</cite>. Improved integration of isotope tracers, high-frequency hydrologic monitoring, and process-based models across event-to-decadal timescales would clarify when leaching is a permanent sink versus a fast, internally cycled flux. <cite id="dc0e3e74-3">Event-type controls on DOC transport fate and river network residence times highlight the need for scale-aware measurements</cite>, and better constraints on freshwater burial and downstream coastal storage would refine estimates of long-term offset. <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">Global freshwater burial rates and DOM–mineral interactions remain key sources of uncertainty for net ecosystem accounting</cite>. In the meantime, empirical patterns from contrasting systems show that leaching is neither universally a net loss nor always fully offset: it redistributes carbon through fast aquatic pathways and can sequester a portion in sediments, with the net ecosystem outcome shaped by productivity, hydrology, and land-use connectivity. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Leaching’s fraction of NEE varies by ecosystem and hydrology</cite><cite id="b86345ee-4">and is tightly coupled to runoff and NPP</cite><cite id="dc0e3e74-1">with rivers acting as active reactors and conduits</cite><cite id="dc0e3e74-4">and inland waters burying a notable share of terrestrial carbon</cite>.

Title: A high-resolution carbon balance in a small temperate catchment: Insights from the Schwabach River, Germany
Snippet: Riverine fluxes of terrestrial carbon to the ocean represent a major link in the global carbon cycle, and much research has focused on clarifying fluvial carbon budgets worldwide (Aufdenkampe et al., 2011;Battin et al., 2009;Cole et al., 2007;Hope et al., 1994;Sawakuchi et al., 2017). However, watershed carbon flux estimates are subject to large uncertainties, of which an incomplete knowledge of riverine carbon dynamics plays a large part (Meybeck, 1993;Raymond et al., 2013;Wehrli, 2013). While the primary importance of rivers in carbon cycling lies in their linkage of terrestrial and oceanic reservoirs, carbon within river waters are also subject to in-situ production, consumption, and loss (Cole et al., 2007;Orozco-Durán et al., 2015;Ward et al., 2017). Complex interrelationships between these processes, and carbon phase changes within river waters, can make riverine carbon budgets difficult to constrain. This gap in knowledge is even greater with regard to smaller rivers, particularly headwater streams, for which information on regional fluvial carbon cycles is sparse. However, headwater streams play an important role in regional and global carbon cycle dynamics as they are the primary source of groundwater and soil-derived carbon. Several studies suggest that particularly large amounts of CO2 evade to the atmosphere by networks of smaller streams and rivers due to elevated DIC concentrations, higher gas transfer velocities, and the large cumulative global surface areas encompassed by lower-order streams (Lauerwald et al., 2015;Lee et al., 2013;Raymond et al., 2013). However, despite the relative significance of CO2 evasion in small rivers and streams, the quantification of these contributions remains largely uncertain (Cole et al., 2007). 

River waters contain both organic and inorganic carbon, either in dissolved or particulate form. Dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) can be sourced from carbonate or silicate weathering, in-situ biological respiration, or soil-respired carbon. In addition to DIC transport and sediment storage, a large proportion of aquatic DIC is lost as CO2 before river waters reach the oceans.

Title: Dissolved Carbon Transport and Processing in North America’s Largest Swamp River Entering the Northern Gulf of Mexico
Snippet: Large rivers play an important role in the global carbon cycling, acting not only as conduits of terrestrial carbon from land to sea, but also as active systems for carbon transformation and processing [1,2]. Riverine dissolved carbon has two primary forms: Dissolved organic carbon (DOC), which includes decaying organic material (<0.45 µm) varying greatly in molecular weight and bioavailability; and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), which is the sum of inorganic carbon (CO 2 , CO 3 2− , and HCO 3 − ) and is derived largely from aerobic respiration (both in runoff from soil and as an in-stream process) and mineral weathering [3]. Recent studies found that wetlands in tropical floodplains of the central Amazon [4] and Zambezi River basin [5] contributed large inputs of inorganic carbon into the river waters, while other studies have demonstrated varying effects of floodplain interactions on DOC [6][7][8]. It is, however, not yet clear to what degree extensive floodplains in temperate and subtropical regions affect riverine dissolved carbon fluxes. Riverine DOC is often partly mineralized in-stream to produce DIC. DIC can be taken up through photosynthesis to produce new organic matter, or can be lost or gained through atmospheric exchange. River systems have been reported to discharge annually a total of 0.17 to 0.78 Pg DOC [9][10][11][12][13] and 0.38 to 2.6 Pg DIC into the world's oceans [13][14][15][16]. At the same time, a global net evasion of CO 2 from all fluvial sources to the atmosphere has been estimated to range from 0.26-1.8 Pg C each year [2,[17][18][19][20][21]. These large variations of riverine dissolved carbon fluxes demonstrate that, while it has been widely acknowledged that the quality and quantity of endmember carbon exported from rivers to oceans can have profound effects on the carbon cycling in coastal ecosystems, many measurement gaps and uncertainties exist in current estimates of carbon exports for many coastal rivers in the world.
</snippet>

The potential for rivers to alter global carbon fluxes has been highlighted in the last few decades, and of particular interest is the reactivity and fate of DOC and especially whether rivers transport or modify carbon (passive pipes or active reactors sensu Cole et al. 2007). The type of hydrological event (e.g., large storms, episodic events, snowmelt) appears to be an important factor driving whether or not DOC is transported conservatively down the river network (Raymond et al. 2016). Indeed, the fate and reactivity of DOC along a river network is controlled by in-stream processing which is driven in large part by hydrology as measured using estimations of water residence time (Catal an et al. 2016 andin this issue Casas-Ruiz et al. 2017). Even so, rivers can deliver a substantial source of aged terrestrial dissolved and particulate organic carbon to the oceans (Raymond and Bauer 2001). Using carbon isotopes, Xue et al. (2017) find that with increasing river discharge the transport and export of millennial-aged DOC and particulate organic carbon in the Yellow River also increases. The authors conclude that the millennial-aged organic carbon exported into coastal seas by the Yellow River can thus have profound impacts for carbon cycling in the coastal and marginal areas of seas. Drought and flooding can play an important role in the carbon dynamics of estuarine systems as found in the study of Yao and Hu (2017). By focusing on the carbonate system response in the Mission-Aransas estuary, a subtropical estuary in the Gulf of Mexico, the authors report notable removal of dissolved inorganic carbon during the drought period and in particular higher pCO 2 levels leading to higher CO 2 flux to atmosphere compared to flood conditions. The authors conclude that although modest pCO 2 levels are found in this estuary, it remains a source of atmospheric CO 2 mainly because of strong winds and warm conditions throughout the year.
