A recent estimate suggests terrestrial export of 5.1 Pg C yr −1 , out of which only 0.95 Pg C yr −1 reaches the oceans (Drake et al. 2018). The majority of terrestrial input of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) is thus removed by microbial and/or photochemical degradation (Molot and Dillon 1997;Algesten et al. 2003), resulting in substantial emissions of CO 2 (Raymond et al. 2013) and CH 4 (Bastviken et al. 2011) to the atmosphere, or is re-directed and stored in the sediment (von Wachenfeldt and Tranvik 2008). Global estimates of carbon burial rates in freshwater sediments vary between 0.2 and 6 Pg C yr −1 for lakes, ponds and reservoirs (Cole et al. 2007;Tranvik et al. 2009), and up to 1.6 Pg C yr− 1 , if sedimentation in floodplains is also included (Regnier et al. 2013). Title: Hydrological and ecological controls on dissolved carbon concentrations in groundwater and carbon export to surface waters in a temperate pine forest watershed
Snippet: The C fixed by NPP enters into the soil as organic carbon through mortality and litterfall, root detritus and root exudates (Davidson and Janssens, 2006). The soil carbon is utilized by heterotrophic organisms which respiration is called heterotrophic respiration (Raich and Schlesinger, 1992). Thereafter, soils can lose carbon from export through hydrological processes (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological processes consist in surface erosion through surface runoff, channel erosion of streams and rivers as well as lateral drainage (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological C export is generally controlled by basin slope, rainfall intensity, river flow intensity and lithology. Furthermore, soils can lose carbon in groundwaters through vertical leaching. 

Thus, drainage of groundwater enriched in dissolved carbon acts as an important source of CO 2 degassing (Venkiteswaran et al., 2014). However, dynamics on how soil carbon interacts with underlying groundwater is poorly documented. 

In this study, we focused on dissolved carbon (inorganic [DIC] and organic [DOC]) dynamics in groundwater and associated streams draining a temperate pine forest watershed. We investigated what controls dissolved carbon temporal storage in groundwater and carbon export to superficial waters, including hydrological factors (precipitation, evapotranspiration, water table, drainage) and ecological factors (net ecosystem exchange, gross primary production, ecosystem respiration). We selected as main study site a forest plot, located in a small temperate watershed which offers the convenience of a relatively homogeneous lithology (sand) and vegetation (pine forest), as well as a simple hydrological functioning (outputs mainly as groundwater drainage; no surface runoff). We aimed to describe the factors controlling the leaching of carbon from the soil to groundwater as well as the export of carbon from groundwater to streams.

Title: Comparing soil carbon loss through respiration and leaching under extreme precipitation events in arid and semiarid grasslands
Snippet: Soils store approximately 2500 Pg of carbon (including organic and inorganic carbon) globally, equivalent to 3.3 and 4.5 times the carbon in the atmosphere (760 Pg) and terrestrial plants (560 Pg), respectively (Lal, 2004). Slight variations in the soil carbon pool will hence severely influence atmospheric CO 2 concentrations and have important implications for climate change (Davidson and Janssens, 2006;Trumbore and Czimczik, 2008). Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss. While respiration has received considerable research attention (Raich and Schlesinger, 1992;Raich and Potter, 1995;Hoover et al., 2016;Burri et al., 2015;Escolar et al., 2015), leaching is relatively poorly constrained despite its importance in certain ecosystems (Cole et al., 2007;Battin et al., 2008;Liu et al., 2017). For instance, soil carbon leached from forests, grasslands, and croplands is estimated to be 15.1, 32.4, and 20.5 g C m −2 yr −1 across Europe, representing 4, 14, and 8 % of net ecosystem exchange (NEE), respectively (Kindler et al., 2011). Additionally, leaching of carbon previously preserved in surface litter and soil layers is believed to be a main source of dissolved organic and inorganic matter Published by Copernicus Publications on behalf of the European Geosciences Union. 

T. Liu et al.: Comparing soil carbon loss through respiration in inland waters (Spencer et al., 2008). In particular, soil inorganic carbon (SIC) that occurs widely in arid and semiarid regions is more prone to leaching than organic carbon during sporadic high precipitation events (Lal and Kimble, 2000). Despite the importance of leaching loss in regional soil carbon budgets, very little detailed data exists to investigate and compare the relative contribution of respiration and leaching processes to soil carbon loss.

Title: Controls on fluxes and export of dissolved organic carbon in grasslands with contrasting soil types
Snippet: Export of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from grassland ecosystems can be an important C flux which directly affects ecosystem C balance since DOC is leached from the soil to the groundwater. DOC fluxes and their controlling factors were investigated on two grassland sites with similar climatic conditions but different soil types (Vertisol vs. Arenosol) for a 2.5-year period. Parts of both grasslands were disturbed by deep ploughing during afforestation. Contrary to what was expected, ploughing did not increase DOC export but surface soil DOC concentrations decreased by 28% (Vertisol) and 14% (Arenosol). DOC flux from the soil profile was negatively influences by the clay content of the soil with seven times larger DOC export in the clay-poor Arenosol (55 kg C ha−1 a−1) than in the clay-rich Vertisol (8 kg C ha−1 a−1). At the Arenosol site, highest DOC concentrations were measured in late summer, whereas in the Vertisol there was a time lag of several months between surface and subsoil DOC with highest subsoil DOC concentrations during winter season. DOC export was not correlated with soil organic carbon stocks. Large differences in 14C concentrations of 22–40 pMC between soil organic carbon and DOC in the subsoil indicated that both C pools are largely decoupled. We conclude that DOC export at both sites is not controlled by the vegetation but by physicochemical parameters such as the adsorption capacity of soil minerals and the water balance of the ecosystem. Only in the acidic sandy Arenosol DOC export was a significant C flux of about 8% of net ecosystem production.

Summary
Leaching of dissolved organic and inorganic carbon (DOC/DIC) from soils to waters is an export pathway that can represent a net carbon loss for terrestrial ecosystems, but its impact is often offset by coupled biogeochemical processes that recycle, retain, or sequester carbon within the soil–water continuum. The net ecosystem outcome depends on the balance among net primary production (NPP), heterotrophic respiration, hydrology-driven export, in-stream mineralization/CO2 evasion, and burial in sediments and coastal systems. Across ecosystems, leaching can account for a measurable fraction of net ecosystem exchange (NEE), sometimes as high as a few to tens of percent, but substantial in-stream processing and episodic hydrologic events can either amplify losses or promote retention and burial, making the system response context-dependent. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss, with leaching representing 4–14% of NEE in forests, grasslands, and croplands across Europe</cite><cite id="b86345ee-3">Isotopic tracking found that 75% of CO2 exiting soil via groundwater mass flow was recent photosynthate, and although this leached carbon was only 2% of annual net carbon fixed, losses could reach ~9% in wetter years</cite><cite id="b86345ee-4">Modeling suggests a historical global terrestrial DOC leaching of ~250 Tg C yr−1 with strong coupling to runoff and NPP</cite>.

What leaching is and its measured magnitudes
Leaching refers to the export of dissolved carbon (organic and inorganic) from soils into groundwater and surface waters via vertical diffusion and preferential flow, and it represents one of two principal soil carbon losses alongside respiratory CO2 release. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Respiration and leaching are two main processes responsible for soil carbon loss, with leaching particularly important in forests, grasslands, and croplands</cite><cite id="b86345ee-2">Soils lose carbon via surface runoff, channel erosion, lateral drainage, and vertical leaching to groundwaters</cite>. At the ecosystem scale, leaching fluxes are substantial: <cite id="b86345ee-0">across Europe, leaching rates of 15.1, 32.4, and 20.5 g C m−2 yr−1 in forests, grasslands, and croplands corresponded to 4, 14, and 8% of NEE, respectively</cite>. Hydrology and climate modulate these losses: <cite id="b86345ee-3">seasonal drought followed by heavy rains in boreal Finland increased leaching from 7.5 to 15.5 mg L−1, driving a fivefold increase in watershed losses from 1700 to 9400 tonnes C</cite>, and <cite id="b86345ee-4">global simulations show a strong positive correlation between runoff and DOC leaching (R2 = 0.75) and that boreal zones exhibit the largest relative increases due to runoff changes</cite>. <cite id="b86345ee-4">Surface soil layers contribute about 90% of total DOC leaching even though they hold only ~40% of soil DOC stocks, highlighting the importance of shallow soils and preferential flow</cite>.

Fate of leached carbon in the inland and coastal continuum
Once exported, dissolved carbon undergoes extensive processing within rivers, estuaries, and coastal zones. <cite id="dc0e3e74-0">Riverine carbon budgets include in-situ production, consumption, and phase changes; small streams and rivers can exhibit large CO2 evasion due to high DIC and gas transfer velocities, though global quantification remains uncertain</cite>. <cite id="dc0e3e74-1">Rivers both transport and transform carbon: DOC is partly mineralized in-stream to DIC, DIC can be fixed photoautotrophically or exchanged with the atmosphere, and global riverine exports range from 0.17–0.78 Pg DOC yr−1 and 0.38–2.6 Pg DIC yr−1 to the oceans, with a net atmospheric CO2 evasion of 0.26–1.8 Pg C yr−1</cite>. Photodegradation and microbial processing rapidly alter DOC: <cite id="dc0e3e74-2">sunlight oxidizes DOC to CO2 and CO, while in-stream processes (photodegradation, flocculation, microbial consumption) and DIC transformations (degassing, photosynthesis, carbonate reactions) control riverine dissolved carbon dynamics</cite>. Hydrology strongly governs fate: <cite id="dc0e3e74-3">the type and intensity of hydrologic events controls whether DOC is transported conservatively or processed; with increasing discharge, export of millennial-aged terrestrial OC increases, indicating that rivers can deliver aged carbon to the ocean</cite>. At the continental scale, much terrestrial carbon is removed before reaching the ocean: <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">only ~0.95 Pg C yr−1 of a terrestrial export of 5.1 Pg C yr−1 reaches the oceans, with the majority of DOC removed by microbial/photochemical degradation, emitted as CO2 and CH4, or buried in sediments</cite>. Freshwater burial can be significant: <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">global lake, pond, reservoir, and floodplain burial rates are estimated between 0.2–6 Pg C yr−1 (with ~0.6 Pg C yr−1 commonly used), and adsorption to mineral particles followed by settling can direct organic carbon to sediments</cite>.

Do coupled processes offset leaching? Evidence from soils, watersheds, and coasts
Coupled processes can offset, amplify, or redistribute leaching losses, depending on ecosystem carbon balance and hydrologic/chemical conditions. First, within the soil–plant system, productivity and heterotrophic processing modulate whether net carbon accrues despite export. <cite id="b86345ee-3">In a boreal forest, 75% of CO2 exiting soil via groundwater mass flow was recent photosynthate, indicating rapid cycling between atmosphere–soil; although this leached carbon was ~2% of annual net fixation, it could reach ~9% under wetter conditions, demonstrating that export can erode but not necessarily overturn a positive NEP</cite>. Second, hydrologic coupling to groundwater and surface waters can either retain or accelerate loss: <cite id="b86345ee-2">drainage of groundwater enriched in dissolved carbon acts as an important source of CO2 degassing, linking soil leaching to atmospheric CO2</cite>, whereas <cite id="b86345ee-4">higher runoff increases DOC leaching, highlighting transport limitation as a key control</cite>. Third, riverine processing redistributes carbon among pools: <cite id="dc0e3e74-1">DIC originating from soil respiration and weathering is often lost as CO2, while a fraction can be respired, photosynthesized, or buried; net CO2 evasion from rivers to atmosphere is substantial</cite>, and <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">microbial and photochemical degradation typically removes most leached DOC before ocean delivery, with burial occurring when particulate/adsorbed carbon settles</cite>. Thus, leaching is not a one-way loss to the atmosphere; rather, it diverts carbon to fast (days–months) biogeochemical loops in rivers and sediments that can result in CO2 evasion, methane emissions, or storage, partially offsetting soil losses.

Fourth, soil carbon formation and hydrologically coupled redistribution can balance leaching over longer timescales. <cite id="b86345ee-3">Proximity of soil to water increased DOC exiting the soil fivefold, but in some cases this reflected long-term groundwater accumulation rather than recent biological activity, indicating that leaching can mobilize legacy soil carbon pools as well as contemporary production</cite>. <cite id="b86345ee-4">Surface soils contribute most leaching but hold only ~40% of soil DOC stocks; this implies that mineral-protected and deeper pools may remain relatively recalcitrant, while frequent leaching of surface carbon can maintain a dynamic balance between formation and export</cite>. In grasslands, for example, <cite id="b86345ee-4">DOC export was a significant C flux of about 8% of net ecosystem production in an acidic sandy soil, illustrating that export can rival internal sequestration in some systems, whereas in clay-rich soils export was small and not correlated with SOC stocks</cite>. Across climate gradients, <cite id="b86345ee-3">drought–wet year dynamics can increase leaching by concentrating easily leached surface carbon during wet periods, implying that interannual variability in hydrology and productivity controls the degree to which losses offset net gains</cite>. Globally, <cite id="b86345ee-4">leaching increases with both NPP and runoff; temperate and subtropical zones show rising leaching mainly with NPP increase, while boreal zones are most sensitive to runoff, underscoring that productivity-driven inputs and hydrologic transport jointly determine net ecosystem balance</cite>.

Net ecosystem outcome: when is leaching a net loss, and when is it offset?
Taken together, leaching is an export pathway that, when unopposed, represents a net carbon loss from terrestrial ecosystems because it removes carbon from soil and biomass pools to be processed in waters and ultimately released to the atmosphere or buried. However, ecosystem carbon budgets integrate coupled processes that can offset or amplify these losses. In carbon-neutral or carbon-negative ecosystems (e.g., high-latitude forests with strong heterotrophy), leaching can erode limited gains or even represent a net loss as respired CO2 is exported to rivers and released to the atmosphere. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Leaching is 14% of NEE in grasslands and 4% in forests in Europe, indicating that export can rival internal carbon sequestration in some ecosystems</cite><cite id="b86345ee-3">and can rise to ~9% under wetter conditions</cite>. In productive, well-drained upland forests, leaching may be a small fraction of NEP and offset by net inputs and soil formation, but during storms or snowmelt, preferential flow can transiently double or triple losses, making the system behave closer to a net exporter during events. <cite id="b86345ee-4">Transport-limited DOC leaching increases with runoff, and surface soils’ disproportionate contribution to leaching implies that hydrologic connectivity and preferential flow can rapidly shift the balance toward export</cite>.

Conversely, in landscapes with strong lateral retention, burial, or rapid biological processing within the watershed, a portion of leached carbon is reincorporated into biomass, sediments, or coastal storage, offsetting the apparent loss. <cite id="dc0e3e74-1">Rivers both transport and transform DOC/DIC, with in-stream mineralization and photosynthesis re-partitioning carbon within the aquatic system</cite><cite id="dc0e3e74-4">and microbial/photochemical degradation and sediment burial removing terrestrial carbon from further atmospheric exchange</cite>. In agricultural and riparian settings, elevated mineral adsorption and settling can promote burial of DOM–mineral complexes, reducing net atmospheric flux from leaching. <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">Adsorption to mineral particles and subsequent settling can direct dissolved organic matter to sediments, where burial rates in inland waters can be substantial</cite>. These coupled processes mean that “leaching” should be viewed as a flux redistribution rather than a simple one-way loss: carbon is cycled through fast aquatic pathways (CO2 evasion, microbial mineralization) or stored in sediments/coasts, and the net ecosystem effect depends on the balance of inputs (NPP), outputs (leaching, respiration, erosion), and in-system transformations.

Timescales, uncertainties, and system gradients
Short-term (event-to-annual) versus long-term (decadal–centennial) perspectives matter. <cite id="b86345ee-3">Isotope studies show that leached CO2 to groundwater is overwhelmingly recent (annual to sub-annual), indicating rapid coupling of terrestrial productivity to aquatic loss</cite>, while <cite id="dc0e3e74-3">increasing discharge can export millennial-aged terrestrial DOC and particulate organic carbon, showing that legacy soil carbon can also be mobilized and delivered to oceans</cite>. Over longer timescales, burial in inland waters and coastal zones can represent a sink for terrestrial carbon, but global estimates are uncertain due to uneven sampling and strong controls by hydrology, chemistry, and land use. <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">Global freshwater burial rates vary widely (0.2–6 Pg C yr−1), with commonly used values of ~0.6 Pg C yr−1 acknowledging large uncertainty; only a small fraction of terrestrial DOC reaches the ocean because most is transformed within river systems</cite>. Importantly, climate and land-use change can shift the balance toward net loss. <cite id="b86345ee-4">Increases in runoff and NPP both enhance DOC leaching, with boreal regions becoming more loss-prone under increased precipitation/snow and forests potentially losing more during higher summer rainfall</cite>, while in cultivated fields near streams, <cite id="b86345ee-3">leaching risks are elevated due to lower carbon inputs and hydrologic connectivity</cite>.

Practical synthesis for the question
- Leaching is a measurable and often non-negligible export pathway that can act as a net carbon loss when respiratory CO2 and DOC/DIC are delivered to waters and subsequently mineralized or degassed. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Across Europe, leaching is 4–14% of NEE in major land covers</cite><cite id="b86345ee-3">and can reach ~9% in wet years</cite>. 
- However, coupled processes frequently offset this loss: in-stream and photodegradative mineralization redistribute carbon among pools, while burial in sediments and coastal systems sequesters a portion; hydrologic connectivity and residence time modulate whether losses dominate or are retained. <cite id="dc0e3e74-1">Rivers transform and transport carbon, with substantial CO2 evasion and variable burial</cite><cite id="dc0e3e74-4">and microbial/photochemical degradation typically removes most leached DOC before ocean delivery</cite>. 
- Whether leaching represents a net loss or offset depends on the ecosystem’s productivity–respiration balance and hydroclimatic regime. In carbon sinks (e.g., productive forests with low heterotrophy), leaching erodes gains; in degraded or arid systems with low productivity and high hydrologic connectivity, leaching can exceed internal sequestration, acting closer to a net loss; in landscapes with strong burial or rapid watershed cycling, a fraction of leached carbon is reincorporated or stored, attenuating the net loss. <cite id="b86345ee-0">Leaching is particularly important in fragile, low-productivity ecosystems</cite><cite id="b86345ee-4">and its magnitude scales with runoff and NPP</cite><cite id="b86345ee-3">with drought–wet year dynamics amplifying losses via accumulation and mobilization of easily leached carbon</cite>. 
- Thus, the correct framing is “leaching is a net carbon loss only to the extent it is not offset by coupled soil carbon formation, in-system biological processing, lateral redistribution, and burial.” <cite id="b86345ee-3">Proximity of soil to water can increase DOC export fivefold, but this carbon can reflect long-term groundwater accumulation rather than recent productivity, evidencing internal cycling and redistribution</cite><cite id="b86345ee-4">and surface soils’ disproportionate role in leaching implies that mineral protection and hydrologic export jointly determine net ecosystem outcomes</cite>.

Key uncertainties and what would resolve them
Quantifying the net effect requires resolving spatially explicit coupling between productivity, hydrology, and in-stream carbon transformations. <cite id="dc0e3e74-0">Uncertainties in riverine carbon budgets stem from incomplete knowledge of in-situ production, consumption, and phase changes, with small streams contributing disproportionately to CO2 evasion</cite>. Improved integration of isotope tracers, high-frequency hydrologic monitoring, and process-based models across event-to-decadal timescales would clarify when leaching is a permanent sink versus a fast, internally cycled flux. <cite id="dc0e3e74-3">Event-type controls on DOC transport fate and river network residence times highlight the need for scale-aware measurements</cite>, and better constraints on freshwater burial and downstream coastal storage would refine estimates of long-term offset. <cite id="dc0e3e74-4">Global freshwater burial rates and DOM–mineral interactions remain key sources of uncertainty for net ecosystem accounting</cite>. Title: Comparing soil carbon loss through respiration and leaching under extreme precipitation events in arid and semiarid grasslands
Snippet: This was partially attributed to the lower NEP and higher SIC content in XLHT and KQ soils, underscoring the fact that soil carbon leaching is more important in fragile ecosystems with low productivity.

If part of this carbon is retained in the surrounding soils or carried along from the river to the ocean in the form of DIC without outgassing into the air, it will not constitute a source of atmospheric CO 2 on a relatively short term (over years or decades). However, soil columns used in our study have a depth (60 cm) typical of or even deeper than the average soil depth in the alpine grasslands of the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau (Wang et al., 2001). Hence, we assume that the carbon leached in our experiments will have minimum retention in the soil. Furthermore, compared to DOC and DIC in the soil solution, the leached carbon is more likely to be subject to more intensified mineralization and outgassing during the land-ocean transfer given more intensified mixing processes, oxygen exposure, and photooxidation of terrestrial carbon upon releasing into the river (Hedges et al., 1997;Battin et al., 2009). Title: Hydrological and ecological controls on dissolved carbon concentrations in groundwater and carbon export to surface waters in a temperate pine forest watershed
Snippet: The C fixed by NPP enters into the soil as organic carbon through mortality and litterfall, root detritus and root exudates (Davidson and Janssens, 2006). Thereafter, soils can lose carbon from export through hydrological processes (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological processes consist in surface erosion through surface runoff, channel erosion of streams and rivers as well as lateral drainage (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Title: Soil carbon in the boreal region under climate and land use change
Snippet: In Finland, a season of drought followed by subsequent annual heavy rains led to higher carbon leaching (e.g. from 7.5 to 15.5 mg L −1 ), causing fivefold higher carbon losses (9400 vs. 1700 tonnes in a 3160 km 2 watershed) (Lepistö et al., 2014). Other studies showed similar or inconclusive results (Allison & Treseder, 2008;Minkkinen et al., 2018), though some suggest that years of drought (or higher temperatures) cause rapid accumulation of easily leached carbon on soil surface, leading in wetter years to higher overall export of carbon. Hence, under climate change, more precipitation/snow at any time may favour losses from wetlands, while higher summer rainfall may favour losses from forests (Köhler et al., 2008). 

An isotopic study that tracked carbon exchange between terrestrial and hydrological environments found that 75% of CO 2 exiting the soil via groundwater mass flow was recent photosynthates (<1 year), indicating that forest carbon is rapidly cycled between atmosphere and soil. This leached carbon only accounted for 2% of the annual net carbon fixed (205 gC m −2 ), though it was postulated that this loss could be up to 9% in a wetter year. Proximity of soil to water increased DOC exiting the soil fivefold (39.2 vs. 7.4 mgC L −1 ), though this carbon reflected long-term accumulation of carbon in deep groundwater rather than recent biological activity (Campeau et al., 2019). We could reasonably expect loss of carbon via groundwater to be limited for many converted boreal soils due to aggressive attempts to drain or level the land. However, farm fields near streams may have greater risk for soil carbon depletion via leaching, given concurrently lower inputs of carbon in many farms.

Title: Leaching of dissolved organic carbon from mineral soils plays a significant role in the terrestrial carbon balance
Snippet: For the period 1861-1870, we estimate an average global terrestrial DOC leaching of 250 Tg C year −1 , which then increases by 35 Tg C year −1 (14%; Figure 9b). Detailing these estimates per major climate zones, we simulated the highest relative increase of 28% in the boreal zone, followed by an increase of 22% in the temperate and 18% in the subtropical zones, and the lowest increase of 9% in the tropical zone (Figure 9). 

Our results show a concomitant increase in global runoff over the historical period of 15.5% (Table S5; Figure S9a) with a significant temporal and spatial correlation between runoff and DOC leaching (R 2 = 0.75 and 0.49 respectively), which can be explained by a strong transport limitation for DOC leaching flux from soils. 

However, the highest relative increase in DOC leaching in the Boreal zone is primarily due to the fact that here the highest increase in runoff is simulated, in line with a recent study in Sweden (Nydahl et. al., 2017). In contrast, the temperate, subtropical and tropical zones show an increase in DOC leaching which appears to be mainly driven by an increase in NPP (Table S4; Figure S9b) and only in the second place by an increase in runoff. 

F I G U R E 7 (a) Global and (b-e) regional C and dissolved organic carbon stocks and fluxes. Units are Gt C and Gt C year −1 for global, and Tg C and Tg C year −1 for regional estimates. Values from Table 2 and Table S2 F I G U R E 8 Ratio of dissolved organic carbon leaching fluxes to (a) terrestrial net primary production (%) and (b) terrestrial net ecosystem productivity (%) TA B L E 2 Global and regional C and dissolved organic carbon (DOC) ratios. DOC, net primary production (NPP) and net ecosystem productivity (NEP) and export ratios  Over the simulation period, surface soil leaching contributes about 90% to total DOC leaching from soil. Title: A high-resolution carbon balance in a small temperate catchment: Insights from the Schwabach River, Germany
Snippet: Riverine fluxes of terrestrial carbon to the ocean represent a major link in the global carbon cycle, and much research has focused on clarifying fluvial carbon budgets worldwide (Aufdenkampe et al., 2011;Battin et al., 2009;Cole et al., 2007;Hope et al., 1994;Sawakuchi et al., 2017). However, watershed carbon flux estimates are subject to large uncertainties, of which an incomplete knowledge of riverine carbon dynamics plays a large part (Meybeck, 1993;Raymond et al., 2013;Wehrli, 2013). While the primary importance of rivers in carbon cycling lies in their linkage of terrestrial and oceanic reservoirs, carbon within river waters are also subject to in-situ production, consumption, and loss (Cole et al., 2007;Orozco-Durán et al., 2015;Ward et al., 2017). Complex interrelationships between these processes, and carbon phase changes within river waters, can make riverine carbon budgets difficult to constrain. This gap in knowledge is even greater with regard to smaller rivers, particularly headwater streams, for which information on regional fluvial carbon cycles is sparse. However, headwater streams play an important role in regional and global carbon cycle dynamics as they are the primary source of groundwater and soil-derived carbon. Several studies suggest that particularly large amounts of CO2 evade to the atmosphere by networks of smaller streams and rivers due to elevated DIC concentrations, higher gas transfer velocities, and the large cumulative global surface areas encompassed by lower-order streams (Lauerwald et al., 2015;Lee et al., 2013;Raymond et al., 2013). However, despite the relative significance of CO2 evasion in small rivers and streams, the quantification of these contributions remains largely uncertain (Cole et al., 2007). 

River waters contain both organic and inorganic carbon, either in dissolved or particulate form. Dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) can be sourced from carbonate or silicate weathering, in-situ biological respiration, or soil-respired carbon. In addition to DIC transport and sediment storage, a large proportion of aquatic DIC is lost as CO2 before river waters reach the oceans.

Title: Dissolved Carbon Transport and Processing in North America’s Largest Swamp River Entering the Northern Gulf of Mexico
Snippet: Large rivers play an important role in the global carbon cycling, acting not only as conduits of terrestrial carbon from land to sea, but also as active systems for carbon transformation and processing [1,2]. Riverine dissolved carbon has two primary forms: Dissolved organic carbon (DOC), which includes decaying organic material (<0.45 µm) varying greatly in molecular weight and bioavailability; and dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC), which is the sum of inorganic carbon (CO 2 , CO 3 2− , and HCO 3 − ) and is derived largely from aerobic respiration (both in runoff from soil and as an in-stream process) and mineral weathering [3]. Recent studies found that wetlands in tropical floodplains of the central Amazon [4] and Zambezi River basin [5] contributed large inputs of inorganic carbon into the river waters, while other studies have demonstrated varying effects of floodplain interactions on DOC [6][7][8]. It is, however, not yet clear to what degree extensive floodplains in temperate and subtropical regions affect riverine dissolved carbon fluxes. Riverine DOC is often partly mineralized in-stream to produce DIC. DIC can be taken up through photosynthesis to produce new organic matter, or can be lost or gained through atmospheric exchange. River systems have been reported to discharge annually a total of 0.17 to 0.78 Pg DOC [9][10][11][12][13] and 0.38 to 2.6 Pg DIC into the world's oceans [13][14][15][16]. At the same time, a global net evasion of CO 2 from all fluvial sources to the atmosphere has been estimated to range from 0.26-1.8 Pg C each year [2,[17][18][19][20][21]. These large variations of riverine dissolved carbon fluxes demonstrate that, while it has been widely acknowledged that the quality and quantity of endmember carbon exported from rivers to oceans can have profound effects on the carbon cycling in coastal ecosystems, many measurement gaps and uncertainties exist in current estimates of carbon exports for many coastal rivers in the world.

Title: Temporal–Spatial Variability of Dissolved Carbon in the Tributary Streams of the Lower Yangtze River Basin
Snippet: Riverine systems are remarkable transport conduits for carbon and nitrogen.A previous long-term monitoring study indicated an increasing trend of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations across most of the northern Hemisphere [1].A large quantity of riverine carbon is transported and transformed into the oceans and the atmosphere.For instance, the global riverine system exported 710 Tg C yr −1 of fluvial carbon into the oceans and emitted 230 Tg yr −1 of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) into the atmosphere [2].Wallin et al. [3] found that CO 2 emissions represent 53% of the carbon flux in rivers, which would be partly due to rapid turnover of DOC.Sunlight, particularly ultraviolet irradiation, oxidizes DOC to lower-weight organic compounds such as CO 2 and carbon monoxide (CO).The loss of dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) through CO 2 degassing from lakes, reservoirs, and rivers represented a remarkable portion of the terrestrial carbon [4].The global methane (CH 4 ) emissions from riverine systems were estimated at 26.8 Tg yr −1 , which was comparable to the emissions from lakes and wetlands [5].However, estimates of dissolved carbon and Water 2022, 14, 4057 2 of 14 related greenhouse gases are highly uncertain due to their temporal and spatial variability.Thus, more integrated measurements are required on various scales.

Dissolved carbon is largely affected by a range of processes in riverine systems.For instance, DOC is derived from in situ production and atmospheric deposition, but it is depleted via photodegradation, flocculation, and microbial consumption.Similarly, DIC is produced by carbonate dissolution, silicate weathering, atmospheric CO 2 invasion, and aquatic and soil respiration, but it is removed by CO 2 emissions to the atmosphere, aquatic photosynthesis, and carbonate mineral reactions [4,6].Furthermore, in farming regions, a source of dissolved carbon to riverine systems is discharge from potential sewage systems.Increasing dissolved carbon concentrations in waters has caused wide concern for public health over the past decades [1].

Factors driving dissolved carbon processes have been widely investigated in riverine system worldwide.DOC concentrations in riverine systems change spatially depending on the catchment geophysical characteristics and depend temporally on climatic patterns.

Title: Headwaters to oceans: Ecological and biogeochemical contrasts across the aquatic continuum
Snippet: Marine end-members covered a broad range of isotopic values (> 3&), thus highlighting the difficulty of using stable isotope mixing models to assess the fate of DOC. 

The potential for rivers to alter global carbon fluxes has been highlighted in the last few decades, and of particular interest is the reactivity and fate of DOC and especially whether rivers transport or modify carbon (passive pipes or active reactors sensu Cole et al. 2007). The type of hydrological event (e.g., large storms, episodic events, snowmelt) appears to be an important factor driving whether or not DOC is transported conservatively down the river network (Raymond et al. 2016). Indeed, the fate and reactivity of DOC along a river network is controlled by in-stream processing which is driven in large part by hydrology as measured using estimations of water residence time (Catal an et al. 2016 andin this issue Casas-Ruiz et al. 2017). Even so, rivers can deliver a substantial source of aged terrestrial dissolved and particulate organic carbon to the oceans (Raymond and Bauer 2001). Using carbon isotopes, Xue et al. (2017) find that with increasing river discharge the transport and export of millennial-aged DOC and particulate organic carbon in the Yellow River also increases. The authors conclude that the millennial-aged organic carbon exported into coastal seas by the Yellow River can thus have profound impacts for carbon cycling in the coastal and marginal areas of seas. Drought and flooding can play an important role in the carbon dynamics of estuarine systems as found in the study of Yao and Hu (2017). By focusing on the carbonate system response in the Mission-Aransas estuary, a subtropical estuary in the Gulf of Mexico, the authors report notable removal of dissolved inorganic carbon during the drought period and in particular higher pCO 2 levels leading to higher CO 2 flux to atmosphere compared to flood conditions. The authors conclude that although modest pCO 2 levels are found in this estuary, it remains a source of atmospheric CO 2 mainly because of strong winds and warm conditions throughout the year.

Snippet: The inland water continuum transports large amounts of carbon from terrestrial to marine systems, and is additionally an important site for the transformation of carbon (Cole et al. 2007). A recent estimate suggests terrestrial export of 5.1 Pg C yr −1 , out of which only 0.95 Pg C yr −1 reaches the oceans (Drake et al. 2018). The majority of terrestrial input of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) is thus removed by microbial and/or photochemical degradation (Molot and Dillon 1997;Algesten et al. 2003), resulting in substantial emissions of CO 2 (Raymond et al. 2013) and CH 4 (Bastviken et al. 2011) to the atmosphere, or is re-directed and stored in the sediment (von Wachenfeldt and Tranvik 2008). Global estimates of carbon burial rates in freshwater sediments vary between 0.2 and 6 Pg C yr −1 for lakes, ponds and reservoirs (Cole et al. 2007;Tranvik et al. 2009), and up to 1.6 Pg C yr− 1 , if sedimentation in floodplains is also included (Regnier et al. 2013). The large uncertainty in these values also stems from an uneven geographic coverage, with a bias towards data from northern latitudes, and the value of 0.6 pg C yr −1 is most commonly used, in spite of the uncertainty (Drake et al. 2018;Regnier et al. 2013). One mechanism by which organic carbon can be directed to the sediment is adsorption to mineral particles and subsequent settling. Snippet: The C fixed by NPP enters into the soil as organic carbon through mortality and litterfall, root detritus and root exudates (Davidson and Janssens, 2006). The soil carbon is utilized by heterotrophic organisms which respiration is called heterotrophic respiration (Raich and Schlesinger, 1992). Thereafter, soils can lose carbon from export through hydrological processes (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological processes consist in surface erosion through surface runoff, channel erosion of streams and rivers as well as lateral drainage (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological C export is generally controlled by basin slope, rainfall intensity, river flow intensity and lithology. Furthermore, soils can lose carbon in groundwaters through vertical leaching. 

Thus, drainage of groundwater enriched in dissolved carbon acts as an important source of CO 2 degassing (Venkiteswaran et al., 2014). However, dynamics on how soil carbon interacts with underlying groundwater is poorly documented. 

In this study, we focused on dissolved carbon (inorganic [DIC] and organic [DOC]) dynamics in groundwater and associated streams draining a temperate pine forest watershed. We investigated what controls dissolved carbon temporal storage in groundwater and carbon export to superficial waters, including hydrological factors (precipitation, evapotranspiration, water table, drainage) and ecological factors (net ecosystem exchange, gross primary production, ecosystem respiration). We selected as main study site a forest plot, located in a small temperate watershed which offers the convenience of a relatively homogeneous lithology (sand) and vegetation (pine forest), as well as a simple hydrological functioning (outputs mainly as groundwater drainage; no surface runoff). We aimed to describe the factors controlling the leaching of carbon from the soil to groundwater as well as the export of carbon from groundwater to streams.

Title: Controls on fluxes and export of dissolved organic carbon in grasslands with contrasting soil types
Snippet: Export of dissolved organic carbon (DOC) from grassland ecosystems can be an important C flux which directly affects ecosystem C balance since DOC is leached from the soil to the groundwater. DOC fluxes and their controlling factors were investigated on two grassland sites with similar climatic conditions but different soil types (Vertisol vs. Arenosol) for a 2.5-year period. Parts of both grasslands were disturbed by deep ploughing during afforestation. Contrary to what was expected, ploughing did not increase DOC export but surface soil DOC concentrations decreased by 28% (Vertisol) and 14% (Arenosol). DOC flux from the soil profile was negatively influences by the clay content of the soil with seven times larger DOC export in the clay-poor Arenosol (55 kg C ha−1 a−1) than in the clay-rich Vertisol (8 kg C ha−1 a−1). At the Arenosol site, highest DOC concentrations were measured in late summer, whereas in the Vertisol there was a time lag of several months between surface and subsoil DOC with highest subsoil DOC concentrations during winter season. DOC export was not correlated with soil organic carbon stocks. Large differences in 14C concentrations of 22–40 pMC between soil organic carbon and DOC in the subsoil indicated that both C pools are largely decoupled. We conclude that DOC export at both sites is not controlled by the vegetation but by physicochemical parameters such as the adsorption capacity of soil minerals and the water balance of the ecosystem. Only in the acidic sandy Arenosol DOC export was a significant C flux of about 8% of net ecosystem production.

attempts.answer:
Summary
Plot-scale leaching measurements quantify carbon exported from canopies and soils via throughfall, stemflow, forest-floor leachate, and in situ soil solution or lysimeter fluxes. These measurements are directly relevant to ecosystem-scale carbon loss when ecosystems lose carbon primarily by aqueous export and soil CO2 efflux is modest relative to aquatic losses, but they require careful hydrologic and temporal interpretation and complementary watershed data to represent whole-ecosystem loss. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Throughfall and related canopy pathways entrain carbon from leaves and bark and deliver it to soils before conveyance to fluvial networks in forests</cite> and <cite id="b498bb70-1">stemflow and throughfall DOC concentrations (5–200 and 1–100 mg C L−1, respectively) exceed rainwater by orders of magnitude, enhance decomposition, and correlate with forest-floor DOC fluxes</cite>. <cite id="b498bb70-4">Soil DOC derived from throughfall, litter, root exudates, and mineralization can be leached to groundwater or transported to streams, potentially altering regional and global carbon cycles</cite>. Ecosystem-scale loss is partitioned among lateral particulate export (dominated by runoff and erosion), dissolved organic carbon leaching, groundwater discharge and baseflow to streams, and gaseous CO2 exchange; plot leaching fluxes map onto some, but not all, of these terms. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Runoff strongly controls lateral DOC and particulate organic carbon (POC) movement, with global terrestrial POC export to oceans ~160 Mt C yr−1 and sensitivity to rainfall and land cover</cite>, while <cite id="2f01250c-2">groundwater-drainage leaching of dissolved carbon and its export can represent a small but non-negligible fraction of ecosystem carbon exchange, with much of the exported CO2 degassing in streams</cite>.

What plot-scale leaching measures and why it matters
Throughfall and stemflow are enriched in canopy-derived carbon and nutrients relative to rainfall and act as spatially localized subsidies to the forest floor and soils. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Precipitation passing through canopies becomes enriched in carbon and nutrients from leaf and bark surfaces and subsequently processes in soils before reaching streams</cite>. <cite id="b498bb70-2">Isotopic mass balance shows that canopy leaching contributes ~83% of throughfall DOC in forests, with PM2.5 desorption and rainwater minor contributors</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-1">throughfall and stemflow DOC concentrations are 5–200 and 1–100 mg C L−1, far above rainwater’s 0.3–2 mg C L−1</cite>. These enriched fluxes feed the forest floor and soil solution, where microbial processing increases mineral-associated pools and dissolved carbon pools that can be exported. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Throughfall DOC promotes rapid decomposition and mineralization and increases leaching of DOC from the forest floor</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-4">DOC sources include throughfall/litter/root exudates/mineralization and can be leached to groundwater or transported to streams</cite>. Plot-scale soil solution and lysimeter measurements therefore capture a key pathway of ecosystem carbon loss as dissolved carbon to groundwater and surface waters, while also reflecting canopy subsidies to the soil environment. <cite id="f688305b-1">Throughfall and stemflow can account for large fractions of inputs to forest-floor leachate (e.g., 68% of litter-leachate nutrient flux in one study), with stemflow enriched in concentrations despite small volumes</cite>.

Scale-up to ecosystem loss: pathways and partitioning
Ecosystem-scale carbon loss includes gaseous CO2 exchange (soil and ecosystem respiration), lateral hydrologic export of dissolved and particulate carbon, and groundwater-baseflow discharge. Hydrology governs whether leached carbon is stored, mineralized, or exported. In a small temperate pine watershed with drainage-dominated hydrology, <cite id="2f01250c-2">mean groundwater export of total dissolved carbon represented 1.5% of net ecosystem exchange (NEE), and 30% of this exported carbon returned to the atmosphere as CO2 via stream degassing</cite>. <cite id="2f01250c-4">Carbon export averaged 7.5 g C m−2 yr−1 (50% DOC, 50% DIC), with DOC export peaking at high water tables due to contact with organic-rich layers and substantial winter storage followed by mineralization to DIC; about 15% of winter DOC exported as DOC and 85% mineralized to DIC, while DIC peaked in late summer and rapidly degassed in streams</cite>. These results imply that:
- Dissolved carbon exported through groundwater-baseflow is a persistent but modest fraction of ecosystem carbon exchange under many conditions. <cite id="2f01250c-2">Mean groundwater DOC/DIC export was ~1.5% of NEE</cite>.
- Storm-driven contact of runoff with organic layers and high-discharge periods can transiently increase leaching and export of both DOC and POC. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Surface runoff strongly determines lateral DOC and POC movements, and intensified rainfall can increase terrestrial POC exports by enhancing runoff and erosion</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-3">dissolved and particulate carbon inputs to streams occur via plant residues, surface runoff, and percolating water, with strong controls by precipitation, temperature, vegetation, and stream characteristics</cite>.
- Particulate carbon export is often dominated by lateral flow and erosion, while dissolved carbon export reflects soil solution chemistry and groundwater residence times. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Surface runoff and soil erosion are primary controls on lateral movement of biogenic POC</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-4">DOC is produced by decomposition/mineralization and leached to groundwater or transported to streams</cite>.

Do plot measurements represent ecosystem-scale loss?
Plot-scale leaching measurements are a valid proxy for ecosystem-scale leaching loss when:
1) Ecosystem carbon loss is dominated by aqueous pathways. In drainage-dominated watersheds, plot soil solution and throughfall/stemflow fluxes integrate to non-negligible but bounded fractions of ecosystem carbon exchange. <cite id="2f01250c-2">Groundwater-drainage dissolved carbon export averaged ~1.5% of NEE</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-4">mean export ~7.5 g C m−2 yr−1 (split evenly as DOC and DIC)</cite>. If ecosystem respiration is much larger than these numbers, a plot leaching term should be added to whole-ecosystem budgets to avoid underestimating aquatic losses. <cite id="2f01250c-2">About 30% of exported dissolved carbon returned to the atmosphere in first-order streams as CO2</cite>, indicating that a significant fraction of plot-detected dissolved carbon can be gaseous loss at the watershed scale.
2) Throughfall/stemflow/forest-floor leachate capture canopy-to-soil carbon transfer. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Throughfall entrains canopy carbon that soils then process before conveyance to streams</cite>, and <cite id="f688305b-1">throughfall and stemflow explain large shares of forest-floor leachate inputs (e.g., 68%), with stemflow concentrating nutrients and DOM near trunks</cite>. Plot carbon concentrations measured in these fluxes are orders of magnitude higher than rainwater, making them disproportionately important for soil and aquatic chemistry. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Stemflow 5–200 mg C L−1 and throughfall 1–100 mg C L−1 versus rainwater 0.3–2 mg C L−1</cite>.
3) Hydrologic context is represented. Event-based plot data should be weighted or aggregated with rainfall-evapotranspiration-drainage context to estimate annual losses. <cite id="2f01250c-4">Groundwater and stream dissolved carbon residence times varied from one month to several years, with peaks at high water tables and late-summer DIC during heterotrophic conditions</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-1">runoff strongly controls lateral DOC/POC export, which increases with intensified rainfall and is highly sensitive to land cover</cite>. Upscaling often assumes a fraction of precipitation becomes leaching; studies explicitly convert soil solution or lysimeter fluxes to watershed export by multiplying concentration by estimated leaching fractions of precipitation, with sensitivity analyses for the assumed rate. <cite id="2f01250c-1">DOC export was calculated by multiplying concentration by a water leaching rate assumed to be 50% of monthly precipitation, with 25–75% used to bound uncertainty</cite>.
4) Ecosystem carbon pools are not sequestered in mineral-associated soil C. If leached carbon is rapidly sorbed, buried, or stored in mineral-associated organic matter, plot leaching may under-estimate long-term ecosystem loss. Conversely, if plot measurements include mineralization in soil layers, they better represent dissolved carbon that will eventually be exported or degassed. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Throughfall-derived carbon compounds are easily decomposable, increasing leaching of DOC from the forest floor</cite> and <cite id="b498bb70-4">soil DOC forms from throughfall, litter, root exudates, and mineralization can be leached to groundwater or transported to streams</cite>.

When plot leaching under- or over-represents ecosystem loss
Plot leaching can under-represent ecosystem carbon loss when:
- Gaseous CO2 dominates losses and is not measured. <cite id="2f01250c-2">Only ~1.5% of NEE exported through groundwater, with ~30% of that dissolved carbon degassing in streams</cite> implies that most losses are via soil respiration and stream CO2 degassing rather than direct particulate or dissolved export measured by plots. In such cases, plot leaching alone will under-estimate total ecosystem loss.
- Lateral hydrologic bypasses soil solution. In steep, thin-soil systems with rapid subsurface stormflow or macropore drainage, carbon can bypass soils and be exported as particulate or dissolved load without first entering the soil solution sampled by plots. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Surface runoff and erosion dominate POC lateral movement, and intensified rainfall increases terrestrial POC export</cite>, while <cite id="2f01250c-3">lysimeter-collected soil solution represents water and nutrients to which plants have direct access; relationships to transpired water can vary with access to storage and interflow</cite>.
- Time scales mismatch. Event-based plot leaching captures storm pulses that may account for a disproportionate share of annual export, whereas continuous ecosystem fluxes (NEE, soil respiration) are steady-state. <cite id="2f01250c-4">DOC peaks at high water tables and is often stored and later mineralized; DIC peaks under late-summer heterotrophy and rapidly degasses</cite>.
- DOM processing alters carbon “identity.” Canopy leaching delivers easily decomposable DOM that is subsequently mineralized to DIC in groundwater or streams, so plot DOC may represent a transient pool that ultimately becomes gaseous CO2 rather than particulate export. <cite id="b498bb70-2">Canopy leaching is the dominant source of throughfall DOC (83%), which is labile and supports microbial processing</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-2">differences in dissolved carbon concentrations between groundwater and streams arise from respiration of DOC in groundwater and CO2 degassing in streams</cite>.

How to use plot leaching to estimate ecosystem-scale loss
Two complementary strategies emerge from the literature:
1) Mechanistic watershed budgeting. Combine plot-based soil solution/throughfall/stemflow concentrations with hydrologic measurements (rainfall, ET, drainage, groundwater table) to compute annual leaching fluxes and partition between DOC and DIC, then compare to NEE and stream gas exchange. <cite id="2f01250c-0">Watershed studies integrate net ecosystem exchange, groundwater and stream dissolved carbon concentrations, and hydrologic measurements to show hydrologic controls on leaching and export</cite>, and <cite id="2f01250c-4">demonstrate mean dissolved carbon export of 7.5 g C m−2 yr−1 with 50/50 DOC/DIC and strong seasonality, while only 1.5% of NEE exported via groundwater with 30% degassing in streams</cite>. This approach explicitly quantifies the fraction of ecosystem carbon that travels via aqueous pathways and where it ends up (soil CO2, stream CO2, particulate export).
2) Empirical scaling factors and uncertainty bounds. Use plot concentrations and fluxes to estimate watershed export by multiplying concentration by a rainfall-based leaching fraction and testing sensitivity to assumed water percolation/translocation, then cross-check with stream DOC/DIC loads and groundwater CO2 degassing. <cite id="2f01250c-1">Assume a 50% leaching rate of monthly precipitation for converting soil solution/DOC concentrations to export, with 25–75% bounds to capture uncertainty in leaching rates</cite>. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Given the strong dependence of lateral DOC/POC export on runoff and land cover, plot-based scaling should incorporate runoff sensitivity and land-cover controls</cite>. - In steep, humid forests with frequent storms, augment plot leaching with stream suspended POC/DOC loads and event-based CO2 fluxes to capture episodic export. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Surface runoff and erosion control lateral POC export and are sensitive to intensified rainfall</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-3">carbon inputs to streams include runoff and percolating water with strong precipitation and vegetation controls</cite>.
- Treat event-based plot leaching as a flux intensity and weight by rainfall and groundwater table; convert to annual by rainfall-event mass balance or water balance, and propagate uncertainty in leaching fraction and residence time assumptions. <cite id="2f01250c-4">Residence times from minutes to years and seasonal peaks require time-disaggregated aggregation</cite>, and <cite id="2f01250c-1">assumed leaching fractions of 25–75% can span likely true rates</cite>.
- Include microbial processing in soil solution interpretations. Easily decomposable canopy DOM leached to soils will mineralize to DIC and may degas without being exported as particulate carbon, so plot DOC/POC should be interpreted with soil redox and stream pCO2 data. <cite id="b498bb70-2">Throughfall DOC is labile and enhances forest-floor leaching</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-2">DIC/CO2 degassing in streams reflects mineralization downstream</cite>.
- Recognize species and structure controls. Canopy architecture and species composition strongly modulate throughfall/stemflow chemistry and leaching capacity; extrapolation beyond plot conditions can bias scale-up. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Throughfall/soil chemistry and nutrient inputs vary with canopy morphology and species, with seasonality and climate</cite>, and <cite id="f688305b-1">throughfall and stemflow contribute most to litter leachate nutrient fluxes, with stemflow highly enriched</cite>.

Bottom line
Plot-scale leaching measurements are directly relevant to ecosystem-scale carbon loss and can represent a significant, quantifiable component when appropriately scaled and contextualized, but they do not, by themselves, capture the entire ecosystem loss. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Throughfall delivers canopy carbon to soils and streams</cite> and <cite id="b498bb70-1">throughfall/stemflow DOC concentrations are orders higher than rainwater, driving forest-floor leaching and lateral export controls by runoff</cite>, yet <cite id="2f01250c-2">in a small forested watershed, groundwater-drainage dissolved carbon export averaged ~1.5% of NEE, with ~30% of that exported carbon degassing in streams</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-4">mean dissolved carbon export ~7.5 g C m−2 yr−1 across a drainage-dominated watershed</cite>. If ecosystem respiration dominates, plot leaching underestimates total loss unless complemented by soil CO2 and stream gas fluxes; if hydrologic export dominates, plot measurements plus stream/groundwater gas and particulate loads provide a complete budget. <cite id="2f01250c-2">Only a fraction of exported dissolved carbon remains dissolved at the stream; much is converted to CO2 and released</cite> and <cite id="b498bb70-1">POC export is primarily controlled by runoff and erosion, which plot measurements may miss if hydrologic bypass occurs</cite>. Thus, plot-scale leaching can represent ecosystem-scale carbon loss when embedded in a watershed carbon budget that integrates hydrology, soil respiration, and aquatic gas exchange, with explicit treatment of event vs. steady-state dynamics and species/structure controls. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Accounting for canopy and litter leaching pathways and their interaction with hydrologic regimes is essential to scale from plots to watersheds</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-0">integrating NEE, groundwater and stream dissolved carbon, and hydrologic drivers clarifies how much ecosystem carbon is lost via leaching pathways</cite>.

Throughfall and stemflow are critical components of the hydrological and biogeochemical cycles of forest ecosystems, as they are the main pathways for transferring precipitation, solutes, organic matter, and microorganisms from the phyllosphere (aboveground surfaces of plants) to the pedosphere (Levia & Frost, 2006;Parker, 1983;Van Stan & Stubbins, 2018). Inorganic nutrients are essential or beneficial to fundamental physiological processes of plant metabolism, plant growth and fitness, and soil fertility (Marschner, 2011;Parker, 1983;Schulze et al., 2019). Precipitation passing through the canopy as throughfall and flowing along stems as stemflow becomes enriched in microand macronutrients (Staelens et al., 2007). Another important ecosystem compartment in the internal nutrient cycle is the forest floor.

Solution collected underneath the forest floor (forest floor leachate) is often greatly enriched in nutrients compared to bulk precipitation and canopy water fluxes due to the leaching of nutrients from organic matter (Batjes, 1996). Nutrient transfer to the soil by throughfall deposition and forest floor leachates is an important input pathway, particularly in ecosystems where nutrient return through litterfall decomposition is slow (van Langenhove et al., 2020;Will, 1959) and in ecosystems with low soil nutrient availability (Forti & Moreira-Nordermann, 1991;Moslehi et al., 2019;Parker, 1983).

The magnitude of nutrient concentration and fluxes in throughfall, stemflow, and forest floor leachate are the result of the interaction of several variables, including meteorological conditions (Dunkerley, 2014), seasonality (Macinnis-Ng et al., 2014), intra-and interspecies differences among tree species (Lilienfein & Wilcke, 2004;Schroth et al., 1999) and vegetation structure (Crockford & Richardson, 2000;Levia & Herwitz, 2002). Title: Hydrological and ecological controls on dissolved carbon concentrations in groundwater and carbon export to surface waters in a temperate pine forest watershed
Snippet: The C fixed by NPP enters into the soil as organic carbon through mortality and litterfall, root detritus and root exudates (Davidson and Janssens, 2006). The soil carbon is utilized by heterotrophic organisms which respiration is called heterotrophic respiration (Raich and Schlesinger, 1992). Thereafter, soils can lose carbon from export through hydrological processes (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological processes consist in surface erosion through surface runoff, channel erosion of streams and rivers as well as lateral drainage (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological C export is generally controlled by basin slope, rainfall intensity, river flow intensity and lithology. Furthermore, soils can lose carbon in groundwaters through vertical leaching. 

Thus, drainage of groundwater enriched in dissolved carbon acts as an important source of CO 2 degassing (Venkiteswaran et al., 2014). However, dynamics on how soil carbon interacts with underlying groundwater is poorly documented. 

In this study, we focused on dissolved carbon (inorganic [DIC] and organic [DOC]) dynamics in groundwater and associated streams draining a temperate pine forest watershed. We investigated what controls dissolved carbon temporal storage in groundwater and carbon export to superficial waters, including hydrological factors (precipitation, evapotranspiration, water table, drainage) and ecological factors (net ecosystem exchange, gross primary production, ecosystem respiration). We selected as main study site a forest plot, located in a small temperate watershed which offers the convenience of a relatively homogeneous lithology (sand) and vegetation (pine forest), as well as a simple hydrological functioning (outputs mainly as groundwater drainage; no surface runoff). We aimed to describe the factors controlling the leaching of carbon from the soil to groundwater as well as the export of carbon from groundwater to streams.

Title: Hydrological and ecological controls on dissolved carbon concentrations in groundwater and carbon export to surface waters in a temperate pine forest watershed
Snippet: Export of soil carbon to superficial water through the drainage of groundwater is a significant but poorly documented component of the continental carbon budget. We monitored the concentrations of dissolved organic and inorganic carbon (DOC and DIC) in groundwaters and first order streams of a small temperate, forested and sandy watershed where hydrology occurs exclusively through drainage (no surface runoff). The studied watershed was also implemented for continuous measurements of groundwater table, precipitation, evapotranspiration, river discharge, and net ecosystem exchanges of sensible and latent heat fluxes as well as CO 2 . On a monthly basis, we found a good consistency between precipitation and the sum of evapotranspiration, drainage and groundwater storage. DOC and DIC temporary storage in groundwater and export to streams varied drastically during the hydrological cycle, the residence times of these two carbon forms varying from one month to several years. DOC concentrations in groundwater and streams were maximal at high water table and high stream discharge, when the water table reached the superficial organic rich layer of the soil. A large fraction of this winter DOC maximum was temporarily stored and further mineralized to DIC in the groundwater and only about 15 % was exported to streams during winter periods. In contrast, DIC, which was present in majority in the form of dissolved CO 2 in groundwater and streams, was apparently diluted at high water table: DIC concentrations were maximum at low water table and low discharge in late summer and maximum pCO 2 in groundwater corresponded to the late summer period of heterotrophic conditions (i.e., R eco  > GPP). Groundwater DIC peaked in late summer and was followed by a rapid loss of excess CO 2 from stream surface to the atmosphere. Overall, mean carbon export was 7.5 g C m −2  yr −1 (50 % as DOC and 50 % as DIC) and represented only 1.5 % of the NEE. About 65 % of the DIC exported from groundwaters returned to the atmosphere in the form of CO 2 in first order streams.
