Summary
Plot-scale leaching measurements quantify carbon exported from canopies and soils via throughfall, stemflow, forest-floor leachate, and in situ soil solution or lysimeter fluxes. These measurements are directly relevant to ecosystem-scale carbon loss when ecosystems lose carbon primarily by aqueous export and soil CO2 efflux is modest relative to aquatic losses, but they require careful hydrologic and temporal interpretation and complementary watershed data to represent whole-ecosystem loss. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Throughfall and related canopy pathways entrain carbon from leaves and bark and deliver it to soils before conveyance to fluvial networks in forests</cite> and <cite id="b498bb70-1">stemflow and throughfall DOC concentrations (5–200 and 1–100 mg C L−1, respectively) exceed rainwater by orders of magnitude, enhance decomposition, and correlate with forest-floor DOC fluxes</cite>. <cite id="b498bb70-4">Soil DOC derived from throughfall, litter, root exudates, and mineralization can be leached to groundwater or transported to streams, potentially altering regional and global carbon cycles</cite>. Ecosystem-scale loss is partitioned among lateral particulate export (dominated by runoff and erosion), dissolved organic carbon leaching, groundwater discharge and baseflow to streams, and gaseous CO2 exchange; plot leaching fluxes map onto some, but not all, of these terms. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Runoff strongly controls lateral DOC and particulate organic carbon (POC) movement, with global terrestrial POC export to oceans ~160 Mt C yr−1 and sensitivity to rainfall and land cover</cite>, while <cite id="2f01250c-2">groundwater-drainage leaching of dissolved carbon and its export can represent a small but non-negligible fraction of ecosystem carbon exchange, with much of the exported CO2 degassing in streams</cite>.

What plot-scale leaching measures and why it matters
Throughfall and stemflow are enriched in canopy-derived carbon and nutrients relative to rainfall and act as spatially localized subsidies to the forest floor and soils. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Precipitation passing through canopies becomes enriched in carbon and nutrients from leaf and bark surfaces and subsequently processes in soils before reaching streams</cite>. <cite id="b498bb70-2">Isotopic mass balance shows that canopy leaching contributes ~83% of throughfall DOC in forests, with PM2.5 desorption and rainwater minor contributors</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-1">throughfall and stemflow DOC concentrations are 5–200 and 1–100 mg C L−1, far above rainwater’s 0.3–2 mg C L−1</cite>. These enriched fluxes feed the forest floor and soil solution, where microbial processing increases mineral-associated pools and dissolved carbon pools that can be exported. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Throughfall DOC promotes rapid decomposition and mineralization and increases leaching of DOC from the forest floor</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-4">DOC sources include throughfall/litter/root exudates/mineralization and can be leached to groundwater or transported to streams</cite>. Plot-scale soil solution and lysimeter measurements therefore capture a key pathway of ecosystem carbon loss as dissolved carbon to groundwater and surface waters, while also reflecting canopy subsidies to the soil environment. <cite id="f688305b-1">Throughfall and stemflow can account for large fractions of inputs to forest-floor leachate (e.g., 68% of litter-leachate nutrient flux in one study), with stemflow enriched in concentrations despite small volumes</cite>.

Scale-up to ecosystem loss: pathways and partitioning
Ecosystem-scale carbon loss includes gaseous CO2 exchange (soil and ecosystem respiration), lateral hydrologic export of dissolved and particulate carbon, and groundwater-baseflow discharge. Hydrology governs whether leached carbon is stored, mineralized, or exported. In a small temperate pine watershed with drainage-dominated hydrology, <cite id="2f01250c-2">mean groundwater export of total dissolved carbon represented 1.5% of net ecosystem exchange (NEE), and 30% of this exported carbon returned to the atmosphere as CO2 via stream degassing</cite>. <cite id="2f01250c-4">Carbon export averaged 7.5 g C m−2 yr−1 (50% DOC, 50% DIC), with DOC export peaking at high water tables due to contact with organic-rich layers and substantial winter storage followed by mineralization to DIC; about 15% of winter DOC exported as DOC and 85% mineralized to DIC, while DIC peaked in late summer and rapidly degassed in streams</cite>. These results imply that:
- Dissolved carbon exported through groundwater-baseflow is a persistent but modest fraction of ecosystem carbon exchange under many conditions. <cite id="2f01250c-2">Mean groundwater DOC/DIC export was ~1.5% of NEE</cite>.
- Storm-driven contact of runoff with organic layers and high-discharge periods can transiently increase leaching and export of both DOC and POC. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Surface runoff strongly determines lateral DOC and POC movements, and intensified rainfall can increase terrestrial POC exports by enhancing runoff and erosion</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-3">dissolved and particulate carbon inputs to streams occur via plant residues, surface runoff, and percolating water, with strong controls by precipitation, temperature, vegetation, and stream characteristics</cite>.
- Particulate carbon export is often dominated by lateral flow and erosion, while dissolved carbon export reflects soil solution chemistry and groundwater residence times. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Surface runoff and soil erosion are primary controls on lateral movement of biogenic POC</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-4">DOC is produced by decomposition/mineralization and leached to groundwater or transported to streams</cite>.

Do plot measurements represent ecosystem-scale loss?
Plot-scale leaching measurements are a valid proxy for ecosystem-scale leaching loss when:
1) Ecosystem carbon loss is dominated by aqueous pathways. In drainage-dominated watersheds, plot soil solution and throughfall/stemflow fluxes integrate to non-negligible but bounded fractions of ecosystem carbon exchange. <cite id="2f01250c-2">Groundwater-drainage dissolved carbon export averaged ~1.5% of NEE</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-4">mean export ~7.5 g C m−2 yr−1 (split evenly as DOC and DIC)</cite>. If ecosystem respiration is much larger than these numbers, a plot leaching term should be added to whole-ecosystem budgets to avoid underestimating aquatic losses. <cite id="2f01250c-2">About 30% of exported dissolved carbon returned to the atmosphere in first-order streams as CO2</cite>, indicating that a significant fraction of plot-detected dissolved carbon can be gaseous loss at the watershed scale.
2) Throughfall/stemflow/forest-floor leachate capture canopy-to-soil carbon transfer. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Throughfall entrains canopy carbon that soils then process before conveyance to streams</cite>, and <cite id="f688305b-1">throughfall and stemflow explain large shares of forest-floor leachate inputs (e.g., 68%), with stemflow concentrating nutrients and DOM near trunks</cite>. Plot carbon concentrations measured in these fluxes are orders of magnitude higher than rainwater, making them disproportionately important for soil and aquatic chemistry. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Stemflow 5–200 mg C L−1 and throughfall 1–100 mg C L−1 versus rainwater 0.3–2 mg C L−1</cite>.
3) Hydrologic context is represented. Event-based plot data should be weighted or aggregated with rainfall-evapotranspiration-drainage context to estimate annual losses. <cite id="2f01250c-4">Groundwater and stream dissolved carbon residence times varied from one month to several years, with peaks at high water tables and late-summer DIC during heterotrophic conditions</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-1">runoff strongly controls lateral DOC/POC export, which increases with intensified rainfall and is highly sensitive to land cover</cite>. Upscaling often assumes a fraction of precipitation becomes leaching; studies explicitly convert soil solution or lysimeter fluxes to watershed export by multiplying concentration by estimated leaching fractions of precipitation, with sensitivity analyses for the assumed rate. <cite id="2f01250c-1">DOC export was calculated by multiplying concentration by a water leaching rate assumed to be 50% of monthly precipitation, with 25–75% used to bound uncertainty</cite>.
4) Ecosystem carbon pools are not sequestered in mineral-associated soil C. If leached carbon is rapidly sorbed, buried, or stored in mineral-associated organic matter, plot leaching may under-estimate long-term ecosystem loss. Conversely, if plot measurements include mineralization in soil layers, they better represent dissolved carbon that will eventually be exported or degassed. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Throughfall-derived carbon compounds are easily decomposable, increasing leaching of DOC from the forest floor</cite> and <cite id="b498bb70-4">soil DOC forms from throughfall, litter, root exudates, and mineralization can be leached to groundwater or transported to streams</cite>.

When plot leaching under- or over-represents ecosystem loss
Plot leaching can under-represent ecosystem carbon loss when:
- Gaseous CO2 dominates losses and is not measured. <cite id="2f01250c-2">Only ~1.5% of NEE exported through groundwater, with ~30% of that dissolved carbon degassing in streams</cite> implies that most losses are via soil respiration and stream CO2 degassing rather than direct particulate or dissolved export measured by plots. In such cases, plot leaching alone will under-estimate total ecosystem loss.
- Lateral hydrologic bypasses soil solution. In steep, thin-soil systems with rapid subsurface stormflow or macropore drainage, carbon can bypass soils and be exported as particulate or dissolved load without first entering the soil solution sampled by plots. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Surface runoff and erosion dominate POC lateral movement, and intensified rainfall increases terrestrial POC export</cite>, while <cite id="2f01250c-3">lysimeter-collected soil solution represents water and nutrients to which plants have direct access; relationships to transpired water can vary with access to storage and interflow</cite>.
- Time scales mismatch. Event-based plot leaching captures storm pulses that may account for a disproportionate share of annual export, whereas continuous ecosystem fluxes (NEE, soil respiration) are steady-state. <cite id="2f01250c-4">DOC peaks at high water tables and is often stored and later mineralized; DIC peaks under late-summer heterotrophy and rapidly degasses</cite>.
- DOM processing alters carbon “identity.” Canopy leaching delivers easily decomposable DOM that is subsequently mineralized to DIC in groundwater or streams, so plot DOC may represent a transient pool that ultimately becomes gaseous CO2 rather than particulate export. <cite id="b498bb70-2">Canopy leaching is the dominant source of throughfall DOC (83%), which is labile and supports microbial processing</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-2">differences in dissolved carbon concentrations between groundwater and streams arise from respiration of DOC in groundwater and CO2 degassing in streams</cite>.

How to use plot leaching to estimate ecosystem-scale loss
Two complementary strategies emerge from the literature:
1) Mechanistic watershed budgeting. Combine plot-based soil solution/throughfall/stemflow concentrations with hydrologic measurements (rainfall, ET, drainage, groundwater table) to compute annual leaching fluxes and partition between DOC and DIC, then compare to NEE and stream gas exchange. <cite id="2f01250c-0">Watershed studies integrate net ecosystem exchange, groundwater and stream dissolved carbon concentrations, and hydrologic measurements to show hydrologic controls on leaching and export</cite>, and <cite id="2f01250c-4">demonstrate mean dissolved carbon export of 7.5 g C m−2 yr−1 with 50/50 DOC/DIC and strong seasonality, while only 1.5% of NEE exported via groundwater with 30% degassing in streams</cite>. This approach explicitly quantifies the fraction of ecosystem carbon that travels via aqueous pathways and where it ends up (soil CO2, stream CO2, particulate export).
2) Empirical scaling factors and uncertainty bounds. Use plot concentrations and fluxes to estimate watershed export by multiplying concentration by a rainfall-based leaching fraction and testing sensitivity to assumed water percolation/translocation, then cross-check with stream DOC/DIC loads and groundwater CO2 degassing. <cite id="2f01250c-1">Assume a 50% leaching rate of monthly precipitation for converting soil solution/DOC concentrations to export, with 25–75% bounds to capture uncertainty in leaching rates</cite>. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Given the strong dependence of lateral DOC/POC export on runoff and land cover, plot-based scaling should incorporate runoff sensitivity and land-cover controls</cite>. In forests with extensive canopy interception and litter leaching, throughfall/forest-floor leachate fractions can be substantial. <cite id="f688305b-1">Throughfall and stemflow explain 68% of litter leachate nutrient flux in one case, with stemflow concentrating inputs near roots</cite>, supporting the inclusion of canopy-derived leaching in upscaling.

Practical guidance and caveats
- If your plot lies in a drainage-dominated forest with sandy soils and minimal surface runoff, plot soil solution and throughfall/stemflow fluxes provide a reasonable lower bound on ecosystem aquatic carbon loss; include stream CO2 degassing and particulate loads to complete the budget. <cite id="2f01250c-4">DOC mineralization to DIC and rapid stream degassing indicate that dissolved carbon measured in plots can become significant gaseous losses at the watershed scale</cite>.
- In steep, humid forests with frequent storms, augment plot leaching with stream suspended POC/DOC loads and event-based CO2 fluxes to capture episodic export. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Surface runoff and erosion control lateral POC export and are sensitive to intensified rainfall</cite>, and <cite id="b498bb70-3">carbon inputs to streams include runoff and percolating water with strong precipitation and vegetation controls</cite>.
- Treat event-based plot leaching as a flux intensity and weight by rainfall and groundwater table; convert to annual by rainfall-event mass balance or water balance, and propagate uncertainty in leaching fraction and residence time assumptions. <cite id="2f01250c-4">Residence times from minutes to years and seasonal peaks require time-disaggregated aggregation</cite>, and <cite id="2f01250c-1">assumed leaching fractions of 25–75% can span likely true rates</cite>.
- Include microbial processing in soil solution interpretations. Easily decomposable canopy DOM leached to soils will mineralize to DIC and may degas without being exported as particulate carbon, so plot DOC/POC should be interpreted with soil redox and stream pCO2 data. <cite id="b498bb70-2">Throughfall DOC is labile and enhances forest-floor leaching</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-2">DIC/CO2 degassing in streams reflects mineralization downstream</cite>.
- Recognize species and structure controls. Canopy architecture and species composition strongly modulate throughfall/stemflow chemistry and leaching capacity; extrapolation beyond plot conditions can bias scale-up. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Throughfall/soil chemistry and nutrient inputs vary with canopy morphology and species, with seasonality and climate</cite>, and <cite id="f688305b-1">throughfall and stemflow contribute most to litter leachate nutrient fluxes, with stemflow highly enriched</cite>.

Bottom line
Plot-scale leaching measurements are directly relevant to ecosystem-scale carbon loss and can represent a significant, quantifiable component when appropriately scaled and contextualized, but they do not, by themselves, capture the entire ecosystem loss. <cite id="b498bb70-0">Throughfall delivers canopy carbon to soils and streams</cite> and <cite id="b498bb70-1">throughfall/stemflow DOC concentrations are orders higher than rainwater, driving forest-floor leaching and lateral export controls by runoff</cite>, yet <cite id="2f01250c-2">in a small forested watershed, groundwater-drainage dissolved carbon export averaged ~1.5% of NEE, with ~30% of that exported carbon degassing in streams</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-4">mean dissolved carbon export ~7.5 g C m−2 yr−1 across a drainage-dominated watershed</cite>. If ecosystem respiration dominates, plot leaching underestimates total loss unless complemented by soil CO2 and stream gas fluxes; if hydrologic export dominates, plot measurements plus stream/groundwater gas and particulate loads provide a complete budget. <cite id="2f01250c-2">Only a fraction of exported dissolved carbon remains dissolved at the stream; much is converted to CO2 and released</cite> and <cite id="b498bb70-1">POC export is primarily controlled by runoff and erosion, which plot measurements may miss if hydrologic bypass occurs</cite>. Thus, plot-scale leaching can represent ecosystem-scale carbon loss when embedded in a watershed carbon budget that integrates hydrology, soil respiration, and aquatic gas exchange, with explicit treatment of event vs. steady-state dynamics and species/structure controls. <cite id="b498bb70-1">Accounting for canopy and litter leaching pathways and their interaction with hydrologic regimes is essential to scale from plots to watersheds</cite> and <cite id="2f01250c-0">integrating NEE, groundwater and stream dissolved carbon, and hydrologic drivers clarifies how much ecosystem carbon is lost via leaching pathways</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Throughfall as an understudied biogeochemical subsidy of nutrients and carbon in the urban water cycle: perspective and a research agenda
Snippet: Precipitation that moves through tree canopies entrains carbon and nutrients from leaf and bark surfaces. In natural ecosystems, these biogeochemical subsidies to the water cycle are processed by watershed soils before conveyance to fluvial networks. In urban landscapes, however, these subsides of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus may bypass watershed soils and instead drip to impervious surfaces and become part of stormwater flows. In this way, urban throughfall may contribute to the carbon and nutrient loads of urban stormwater, with consequences for receiving waters and potential to contribute to eutrophication. Throughfall from urban landscapes is understudied, but the argument is made here that quantifying and characterizing urban throughfall and how it can be contextualized within the urban water cycle are crucial avenues for new research. This paper presents the hypothesis that as in natural ecosystems, throughfall in urban ecosystems is (1) a source of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus; (2) will vary in concentration and chemical composition depending on climate, tree species, canopy morphology, and seasonality; and (3) will have impacts on urban ecosystems that have not been investigated. snippet.text: Precipitation that moves through tree canopies entrains carbon and nutrients from leaf and bark surfaces. In natural ecosystems, these biogeochemical subsidies to the water cycle are processed by watershed soils before conveyance to fluvial networks. In urban landscapes, however, these subsides of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus may bypass watershed soils and instead drip to impervious surfaces and become part of stormwater flows. In this way, urban throughfall may contribute to the carbon and nutrient loads of urban stormwater, with consequences for receiving waters and potential to contribute to eutrophication. Throughfall from urban landscapes is understudied, but the argument is made here that quantifying and characterizing urban throughfall and how it can be contextualized within the urban water cycle are crucial avenues for new research. Title: Effects of Forest Type on Nutrient Fluxes in Throughfall, Stemflow, and Litter Leachate within Acid-Polluted Locations in Southwest China
Snippet: Nutrients can also be leached from throughfall and stemflow and input into soils [22]. Interception as well as throughfall and stemflow are influenced by many features of the forest type, such as density, branch angle, the uniformity, bark characteristics, leaf shape and leaf area index [23], which are very complicated in forest ecosystems. Further, the chemical enrichment of throughfall and stemflow and nutrient leaching capacity exhibit considerable species-specific variability [24], which further complicates general conclusions on the effects of forest types on water and soil properties, especially under the background of climate change, because forests interact with climate change via albedo, evaporation, the carbon cycle and other factors [25,26]. 

Inputs of acidic anions and other nutrients to the forest floor through precipitation are affected by dry deposition on the canopy and the canopy itself, both of which can alter water chemistry and further affect soil quality. Throughfall and stemflow supply available nutrients to the forest floor, which can affect soil acidity [27], although the volume of stemflow is much less than that of throughfall and often ignored [28]. Before nutrientcarrying throughfall and stemflow enter into the soil, they pass through the layer of forest floor litter (except in areas of bare ground), where nutrients from throughfall, stemflow, and litter combine to form litter leachate, which ultimately affects soil quality. A study in British Columbia confirmed that throughfall and stemflow contribute to higher pH, N availability, and total exchangeable bases in forest floor areas associated with bigleaf maple, which have legacy effects on soil fertility [29]. Forest floor leachate chemistry largely determines biogeochemical processes in the soil and soil solution chemistry, affecting soil acidity and the sustainability of the forest ecosystem [30]. It is necessary and important to account for forest floor leachate in addition to throughfall and stemflow when studying the hydrological effects of rainfall on soil in forested ecosystems. 

The exchange capacity of basic cations and acid anions in forest canopy and litter have strong species specificity [24,27,31,32]. Individual tree species play an important role in the distribution and cycling of nutrients that influence ecosystem function, biodiversity, resistance to stress, and sustainability [33,34].

Title: Effects of Forest Type on Nutrient Fluxes in Throughfall, Stemflow, and Litter Leachate within Acid-Polluted Locations in Southwest China
Snippet: In our study, both cation and anion fluxes in litter leachate were lower than that in throughfall plus stemflow, which indicated an interception of nutrients at the litter layer. To further detect how much throughfall and stemflow influence the nutrient flux of litter leachate, we performed variation portioning analysis (VPA) using cation, anion, and DOC flux. As indicated by VPA, a total of 68% of litter leachate nutrient flux could be explained by throughfall and stemflow. Nutrient flux from throughfall and stemflow respectively contributed 20% and 3% to litter leachate nutrient flux, while their common contribution was 45%. The contribution of throughfall and stemflow to the forest floor has also been confirmed by previous data [29,32]. The relatively small contribution of stemflow observed in this study is supported by Bellot et al. [49], which found that nutrient inputs of stemflow only represented about 2-3% of total dissolved inputs into the soils. Despite the low contribution, stemflow can play an important role in forest ecosystems, as it concentrates water in the area immediately proximal to the tree trunk, providing a supply of water and nutrients to the tree and soil far more so than throughfall [49,50]. 

This present study also indicates that stemflow is enriched with a greater nutrient concentration than throughfall. We found the highest DOC content, cation and anion concentration, and lowest pH value in stemflow, followed by throughfall and litter leachate. Higher concentrations of nutrients in stemflow can be attributed to both nutrients leaching from stems and very low stemflow volume [51]. When we replaced nutrient flux with concentration in VPA analysis, the contribution of stemflow to litter leachates increased from 3% to 9%, which further illustrates the importance of stemflow in influencing nutrient concentrations in the root zone that affect rhizosphere microbial communities and function [52]. Thus, our second hypothesis is partially correct in that throughfall does contribute a greater nutrient flux to the forest floor than stemflow; however, the transient impacts of stemflow are more intensive on the root zone, specifically.

Title: Stemflow dissolved organic matter in mixed temperate forests: temporal and interspecific variation of optical indices and development of a stemflow-specific PARAFAC model
Snippet: Throughfall and stemflow are important pathways for the transfer of water, solutes, and particulates to the forest floor (Parker 1983;Levia et al. 2011Levia et al. , 2023;;Levia and Germer 2015;Siegert et al. 2017;Chen et al. 2019;Cayuela et al. 2019). Similar to throughfall (McDowell et al. 2020), stemflow mediates the Vol:. Nutrients can also be leached from throughfall and stemflow and input into soils [22]. Interception as well as throughfall and stemflow are influenced by many features of the forest type, such as density, branch angle, the uniformity, bark characteristics, leaf shape and leaf area index [23], which are very complicated in forest ecosystems. Further, the chemical enrichment of throughfall and stemflow and nutrient leaching capacity exhibit considerable species-specific variability [24], which further complicates general conclusions on the effects of forest types on water and soil properties, especially under the background of climate change, because forests interact with climate change via albedo, evaporation, the carbon cycle and other factors [25,26]. 

Inputs of acidic anions and other nutrients to the forest floor through precipitation are affected by dry deposition on the canopy and the canopy itself, both of which can alter water chemistry and further affect soil quality. Throughfall and stemflow supply available nutrients to the forest floor, which can affect soil acidity [27], although the volume of stemflow is much less than that of throughfall and often ignored [28]. Before nutrientcarrying throughfall and stemflow enter into the soil, they pass through the layer of forest floor litter (except in areas of bare ground), where nutrients from throughfall, stemflow, and litter combine to form litter leachate, which ultimately affects soil quality. A study in British Columbia confirmed that throughfall and stemflow contribute to higher pH, N availability, and total exchangeable bases in forest floor areas associated with bigleaf maple, which have legacy effects on soil fertility [29]. Forest floor leachate chemistry largely determines biogeochemical processes in the soil and soil solution chemistry, affecting soil acidity and the sustainability of the forest ecosystem [30]. It is necessary and important to account for forest floor leachate in addition to throughfall and stemflow when studying the hydrological effects of rainfall on soil in forested ecosystems. 

The exchange capacity of basic cations and acid anions in forest canopy and litter have strong species specificity [24,27,31,32]. Individual tree species play an important role in the distribution and cycling of nutrients that influence ecosystem function, biodiversity, resistance to stress, and sustainability [33,34].

In our study, both cation and anion fluxes in litter leachate were lower than that in throughfall plus stemflow, which indicated an interception of nutrients at the litter layer. To further detect how much throughfall and stemflow influence the nutrient flux of litter leachate, we performed variation portioning analysis (VPA) using cation, anion, and DOC flux. As indicated by VPA, a total of 68% of litter leachate nutrient flux could be explained by throughfall and stemflow. Nutrient flux from throughfall and stemflow respectively contributed 20% and 3% to litter leachate nutrient flux, while their common contribution was 45%. The contribution of throughfall and stemflow to the forest floor has also been confirmed by previous data [29,32]. The relatively small contribution of stemflow observed in this study is supported by Bellot et al. [49], which found that nutrient inputs of stemflow only represented about 2-3% of total dissolved inputs into the soils. Despite the low contribution, stemflow can play an important role in forest ecosystems, as it concentrates water in the area immediately proximal to the tree trunk, providing a supply of water and nutrients to the tree and soil far more so than throughfall [49,50]. 

This present study also indicates that stemflow is enriched with a greater nutrient concentration than throughfall. We found the highest DOC content, cation and anion concentration, and lowest pH value in stemflow, followed by throughfall and litter leachate. Higher concentrations of nutrients in stemflow can be attributed to both nutrients leaching from stems and very low stemflow volume [51]. When we replaced nutrient flux with concentration in VPA analysis, the contribution of stemflow to litter leachates increased from 3% to 9%, which further illustrates the importance of stemflow in influencing nutrient concentrations in the root zone that affect rhizosphere microbial communities and function [52]. Thus, our second hypothesis is partially correct in that throughfall does contribute a greater nutrient flux to the forest floor than stemflow; however, the transient impacts of stemflow are more intensive on the root zone, specifically.

Title: Hydrological and ecological controls on dissolved carbon concentrations in groundwater and carbon export to surface waters in a temperate pine forest watershed
Snippet: The C fixed by NPP enters into the soil as organic carbon through mortality and litterfall, root detritus and root exudates (Davidson and Janssens, 2006). The soil carbon is utilized by heterotrophic organisms which respiration is called heterotrophic respiration (Raich and Schlesinger, 1992). Thereafter, soils can lose carbon from export through hydrological processes (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological processes consist in surface erosion through surface runoff, channel erosion of streams and rivers as well as lateral drainage (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological C export is generally controlled by basin slope, rainfall intensity, river flow intensity and lithology. Furthermore, soils can lose carbon in groundwaters through vertical leaching. 

Thus, drainage of groundwater enriched in dissolved carbon acts as an important source of CO 2 degassing (Venkiteswaran et al., 2014). However, dynamics on how soil carbon interacts with underlying groundwater is poorly documented. 

In this study, we focused on dissolved carbon (inorganic [DIC] and organic [DOC]) dynamics in groundwater and associated streams draining a temperate pine forest watershed. We investigated what controls dissolved carbon temporal storage in groundwater and carbon export to superficial waters, including hydrological factors (precipitation, evapotranspiration, water table, drainage) and ecological factors (net ecosystem exchange, gross primary production, ecosystem respiration). We selected as main study site a forest plot, located in a small temperate watershed which offers the convenience of a relatively homogeneous lithology (sand) and vegetation (pine forest), as well as a simple hydrological functioning (outputs mainly as groundwater drainage; no surface runoff). We aimed to describe the factors controlling the leaching of carbon from the soil to groundwater as well as the export of carbon from groundwater to streams.

Title: Full carbon and greenhouse gas balances of fertilized and nonfertilized reed canary grass cultivations on an abandoned peat extraction area in a dry year
Snippet: Starting in February 2014, dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations were determined for water samples taken at each flux sampling location from groundwater wells (perforated PVC pipes; Ø 7.5 cm) which collected soil solution from the soil surface down to 50 cm depth. From late June onward, DOC concentrations were estimated at 30 cm soil depth (below the main rooting zone) on every flux sampling date using stainless steel plate lysimeters with a collecting area of 625 cm 2 (Uri et al., 2011). All water samples were analyzed for their DOC concentrations within 1 day after collection. The DOC export was calculated by multiplying the DOC concentration with the water leaching rate which was assumed to be 50% of the monthly precipitation based on previous literature estimates (Kløve et al., 2010;Hyv€ onen et al., 2013). To assess the sensitivity of the annual DOC export to the choice of this assumed leaching rate, DOC export was also estimated using rates of 25% and 75% of the monthly precipitation to provide a minimum-maximum range which very likely encompasses the true leaching rate.

Title: Hydrological and ecological controls on dissolved carbon concentrations in groundwater and carbon export to surface waters in a temperate pine forest watershed
Snippet: The work presented here extends the scope on the interaction between the net productivity of forest ecosystem and the concentrations of dissolved carbon in the underlying groundwater. Using net ecosystem exchange measurements, dissolved carbon concentrations determination in both groundwater and stream water and hydrological measurements, we have shown that main controls of carbon fluxes are from hydrology, in interaction with ecophysiological activity of plants (Tab. 5, Fig. 7). Thus, high water table resulted in larger DIC and DOC exports and the height of water table outcome from the balance between precipitation, evapotranspiration, water storage and drainage, with a notable influence of local topographic heterogeneities. This work also revealed a large difference of dissolved carbon concentrations between groundwaters and stream waters, those differences originates from distinct processes (e.g., respiration of DOC in groundwater, degassing of CO 2 in streams). Finally, we found that mean export of total dissolved carbon through groundwater represents only 1.5 % of the mean NEE, while 30 % of this carbon export returns to the atmosphere in the form of CO 2 through degassing in first order stream waters.

Title: Hydrological and ecological controls on dissolved carbon concentrations in groundwater and carbon export to surface waters in a temperate pine forest watershed
Snippet: Export of soil carbon to superficial water through the drainage of groundwater is a significant but poorly documented component of the continental carbon budget. We monitored the concentrations of dissolved organic and inorganic carbon (DOC and DIC) in groundwaters and first order streams of a small temperate, forested and sandy watershed where hydrology occurs exclusively through drainage (no surface runoff). The studied watershed was also implemented for continuous measurements of groundwater table, precipitation, evapotranspiration, river discharge, and net ecosystem exchanges of sensible and latent heat fluxes as well as CO 2 . On a monthly basis, we found a good consistency between precipitation and the sum of evapotranspiration, drainage and groundwater storage. DOC and DIC temporary storage in groundwater and export to streams varied drastically during the hydrological cycle, the residence times of these two carbon forms varying from one month to several years. DOC concentrations in groundwater and streams were maximal at high water table and high stream discharge, when the water table reached the superficial organic rich layer of the soil. A large fraction of this winter DOC maximum was temporarily stored and further mineralized to DIC in the groundwater and only about 15 % was exported to streams during winter periods. In contrast, DIC, which was present in majority in the form of dissolved CO 2 in groundwater and streams, was apparently diluted at high water table: DIC concentrations were maximum at low water table and low discharge in late summer and maximum pCO 2 in groundwater corresponded to the late summer period of heterotrophic conditions (i.e., R eco  > GPP). Groundwater DIC peaked in late summer and was followed by a rapid loss of excess CO 2 from stream surface to the atmosphere. Overall, mean carbon export was 7.5 g C m −2  yr −1 (50 % as DOC and 50 % as DIC) and represented only 1.5 % of the NEE. About 65 % of the DIC exported from groundwaters returned to the atmosphere in the form of CO 2 in first order streams.

snippet.text:
The C fixed by NPP enters into the soil as organic carbon through mortality and litterfall, root detritus and root exudates (Davidson and Janssens, 2006). The soil carbon is utilized by heterotrophic organisms which respiration is called heterotrophic respiration (Raich and Schlesinger, 1992). Thereafter, soils can lose carbon from export through hydrological processes (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological processes consist in surface erosion through surface runoff, channel erosion of streams and rivers as well as lateral drainage (Dawson and Smith, 2007). Hydrological C export is generally controlled by basin slope, rainfall intensity, river flow intensity and lithology. Furthermore, soils can lose carbon in groundwaters through vertical leaching. 

Thus, drainage of groundwater enriched in dissolved carbon acts as an important source of CO 2 degassing (Venkiteswaran et al., 2014). However, dynamics on how soil carbon interacts with underlying groundwater is poorly documented. 

In this study, we focused on dissolved carbon (inorganic [DIC] and organic [DOC]) dynamics in groundwater and associated streams draining a temperate pine forest watershed. We investigated what controls dissolved carbon temporal storage in groundwater and carbon export to superficial waters, including hydrological factors (precipitation, evapotranspiration, water table, drainage) and ecological factors (net ecosystem exchange, gross primary production, ecosystem respiration). We selected as main study site a forest plot, located in a small temperate watershed which offers the convenience of a relatively homogeneous lithology (sand) and vegetation (pine forest), as well as a simple hydrological functioning (outputs mainly as groundwater drainage; no surface runoff). We aimed to describe the factors controlling the leaching of carbon from the soil to groundwater as well as the export of carbon from groundwater to streams.

snippet.text: Starting in February 2014, dissolved organic carbon (DOC) concentrations were determined for water samples taken at each flux sampling location from groundwater wells (perforated PVC pipes; Ø 7.5 cm) which collected soil solution from the soil surface down to 50 cm depth. snippet.text: The work presented here extends the scope on the interaction between the net productivity of forest ecosystem and the concentrations of dissolved carbon in the underlying groundwater. Using net ecosystem exchange measurements, dissolved carbon concentrations determination in both groundwater and stream water and hydrological measurements, we have shown that main controls of carbon fluxes are from hydrology, in interaction with ecophysiological activity of plants (Tab. 5, Fig. 7). Thus, high water table resulted in larger DIC and DOC exports and the height of water table outcome from the balance between precipitation, evapotranspiration, water storage and drainage, with a notable influence of local topographic heterogeneities. This work also revealed a large difference of dissolved carbon concentrations between groundwaters and stream waters, those differences originates from distinct processes (e.g., respiration of DOC in groundwater, degassing of CO 2 in streams). Finally, we found that mean export of total dissolved carbon through groundwater represents only 1.5 % of the mean NEE, while 30 % of this carbon export returns to the atmosphere in the form of CO 2 through degassing in first order stream waters.
